title: The immune system: how your body keeps germs out and fights them

summary.text: Germs land on your skin all day, yet most of them never get inside you. Germs are tiny living things that can make you ill. The immune system is everything your body does to keep germs out, and to fight the ones that get in. Your first walls are your skin, your tears, the sticky mucus in your nose, your saliva and the acid in your stomach. Germs that get past the walls meet white blood cells, which find them and eat them. A fever is your brain turning up your body's heat to help the fight.
summary.art: A child drawn as a castle: skin as the outer wall, eyelashes and tears at the windows, a sticky moat of mucus at the nose gate, and inside, tiny round white blood cells hurrying along red roads of blood towards a small green germ.

intro.hook: Look at the skin on the back of your hand. Germs are landing on it right now, thousands of them. Most of them never get inside you. What is stopping them?
intro.text: Think of the last time you scraped your knee. First it hurt. Then, a few hours later, the skin around the scrape went pink. It felt warm and a bit puffy. Maybe a little yellow goo came out. Was the scrape getting worse? Or was something inside you rushing to that spot, on purpose? In this unit you will find out. You will meet the defenders that guard your body every second, even while you sleep.
intro.art: A close-up of a child's knee with a small scrape, pink and puffy around the edge, and a magnifying-glass circle showing tiny round cells crowding towards it.

outcomes: I can say what the immune system is: everything the body does to keep germs out and to fight the germs that get in.
I can name the body's first walls (skin, tears, mucus and nose hairs, spit and stomach acid) and say how each one stops germs.
I can explain that white blood cells travel in the blood, find germs and eat them, and that redness, warmth, swelling and pus around a cut are signs of that fight.
I can explain that a fever is the body turning up its own heat to fight germs. I can read a thermometer and say when a grown-up should call a doctor.
I can run a fair test, like the apple skin test, keep a results table and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that most microbes are harmless or helpful, and that the body keeps deciding what belongs and what does not.
I can give deep and wide examples: a tear chemical that breaks germs open, plants and bacteria that defend themselves, sick lizards that warm up on purpose, and things scientists still do not know.

terms.meaning: Everything your body does to keep germs out and to fight the germs that get in. It is not one organ. It is skin, tears, mucus, blood cells and much more, working together.
terms.example: When you have a cold and then get better, your immune system has won the fight.
terms.art: A child's outline with a glowing shield around it and tiny defenders inside.

terms.meaning: A tiny living thing, too small to see, that can make you ill. Most germs are bacteria or viruses. A few are tiny fungi, or other one-celled living things like the malaria germ.
terms.example: The germs of a cold spread when someone sneezes near you.
terms.art: A few cartoon-free, realistic-looking tiny rods and spheres seen through a microscope circle.

terms.meaning: Any living thing too small to see without a microscope. Most microbes are harmless, and many help us. Only a few are germs.
terms.example: Microbes in curd turn milk sour and thick. They are friendly microbes.
terms.art: A bowl of curd with a zoomed circle showing many tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: One kind of microbe. Each one is a single tiny living cell. Bacteria sense what is around them and decide where to go. Many swim towards food. One drop of curd can hold millions of them.
terms.example: The bacteria in curd are friendly. The bacteria that cause typhoid are germs.
terms.art: Rod-shaped and round bacteria under a microscope.

terms.meaning: A tiny germ, much smaller than bacteria. A virus can only make copies inside a living cell.
terms.example: Colds and chickenpox are caused by viruses.
terms.art: A spiky ball shape next to a much bigger bacterium for size.

terms.meaning: The body's outer covering. Its top layer is made of flat, dead cells packed tight, like tiles on a roof. Most germs cannot get through skin that has no cuts.
terms.example: Germs land on your hand all day, but unbroken skin keeps them outside.
terms.art: A cross-section of skin like roof tiles, with germs sitting on top unable to get in.

terms.meaning: The wet, sticky stuff inside your nose and throat. It traps dust and germs before they reach your lungs.
terms.example: When you blow your nose into a hanky, you blow out mucus full of trapped dust and germs.
terms.art: Inside a nose: tiny hairs and a shiny sticky layer with dust specks caught in it.

terms.meaning: Salty water your eyes make all the time, not just when you cry. Every blink spreads tears and washes the eye. Tears also hold a chemical that breaks some germs apart.
terms.example: When a speck of dust lands in your eye, tears wash it out.
terms.art: An eye blinking, with a thin shiny layer of tears washing a dust speck to the corner.

terms.meaning: Spit: the watery juice in your mouth. It washes your teeth and holds chemicals that slow germs down.
terms.example: Your mouth makes more saliva when you smell food cooking.
terms.art: A mouth with a little stream of saliva washing over teeth.

terms.meaning: A very strong, sour juice inside your stomach. It breaks down food and kills many germs that get swallowed.
terms.example: Many of the germs on the food you swallow are killed in your stomach.
terms.art: A stomach shape with bubbling juice and a few germs fading away inside it.

terms.meaning: A tiny cell that travels in your blood and hunts germs. Some kinds eat germs. Other kinds make chemicals that stick to germs, or remember them for next time.
terms.example: When germs get into a cut, white blood cells rush there from the blood.
terms.art: A round, colourless blob of a cell reaching out arms to wrap around a small rod-shaped germ.

terms.meaning: A white blood cell that eats germs. The word comes from Greek words meaning 'eating cell'.
terms.example: Phagocytes swallow germs whole, then break them down inside.
terms.art: Three frames: a blob cell touching a germ, wrapping round the germ, then the germ inside the cell.

terms.meaning: When part of the body goes red, warm, swollen and sore because the immune system is fighting there. Extra blood brings more defenders to that spot.
terms.example: The pink, puffy skin around a new mosquito bite or scrape is inflammation.
terms.art: A finger with a tiny splinter, pink and puffy around it, with small arrows of blood flowing in.

terms.meaning: The thick, yellowish goo that can come out of an infected cut. It is mostly white blood cells that died fighting, mixed with dead germs.
terms.example: A pimple's white tip is pus.
terms.art: A zoomed circle of pus showing many tired round white cells and broken germs.

terms.meaning: The hard, dark crust that forms on a scrape. Dried blood and a sticky mesh seal the hole, so new skin can grow underneath.
terms.example: A scab on your knee falls off by itself when the new skin is ready.
terms.art: A knee scab cut away in a side view, with pink new skin growing below it.

terms.meaning: When the body turns its own heat up higher than usual, often to fight germs. Doctors usually call 38 degrees Celsius or more a fever.
terms.example: With the flu, your temperature might go up to 38.5 degrees Celsius for a day or two.
terms.art: A child in bed with a blanket, a digital thermometer showing 38.5 degrees, and a glass of water.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures how hot something is. A body thermometer measures your temperature in degrees Celsius or degrees Fahrenheit.
terms.example: A digital thermometer under your arm beeps when it has finished measuring.
terms.art: A digital thermometer with a clear screen showing 36.8 degrees Celsius.

terms.meaning: All the microbes that live on your skin, in your mouth and in your gut. Most of them are harmless or helpful.
terms.example: Friendly bacteria on your skin take up the space that germs would like to use.
terms.art: A hand drawn as a busy little town of many tiny friendly microbes.

terms.meaning: A medicine, usually an injection or drops, that shows your immune system a harmless form or a small part of a germ. Your white blood cells learn the germ's shape. If the real germ ever comes, they fight them quickly.
terms.example: Polio drops and the measles injection protect children all over India.
terms.art: A child holding a parent's hand at a clinic, with a nurse giving polio drops, and a small immunisation card on the table.

terms.meaning: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing. Antibiotics do not work on viruses, so they do not cure a cold. Only a doctor should decide when someone needs one.
terms.example: A cold is caused by a virus, so an antibiotic will not help it get better. Rest, water and time do.
terms.art: A medicine strip on one side next to rod-shaped bacteria fading away, and on the other side a spiky virus untouched, with a doctor's stethoscope between.

terms.meaning: How the immune system sorts things. 'Self' means your own cells. 'Not-self' means things from outside, like germs. Scientists are still working out exactly how it decides.
terms.example: Your white blood cells leave your own cells alone, but they attack a germ.
terms.art: A white blood cell gently passing a row of the body's own cells, then reaching for a germ.

explanations.definition: The immune system is everything the body does to keep germs out and to fight the germs that get in.
explanations.description: Germs are everywhere: on door handles, in the air, on your food. Most of the time they cannot hurt you. That is because your body defends itself in layers, like a fort. First come the outer walls, which stop germs getting in at all. Then come the guards inside, the white blood cells, which hunt any germs that slip through. Last, some white blood cells remember a germ, so the next fight is quicker. Scientists call all of this together the immune system.
examples: You touch a dirty railing, and nothing happens, because your skin keeps the germs out.
You catch a cold, feel ill for a few days, then get better. Your immune system fought and won.
Most children get chickenpox only once. The body remembers the germ.
explanations.art: A fort with three rings: an outer wall labelled skin and tears, inner guards labelled white blood cells, and a library at the centre labelled memory.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what the immune system is.

explanations.definition: Skin is the body's outer covering. Its tight, dead top layer is a wall that germs cannot get through unless there is a cut.
explanations.description: Skin is the biggest organ of your body, and it is your first wall. Its top layer is made of flat, dead cells packed tightly together, like tiles on a roof. Germs cannot push through. New cells grow underneath and slowly move up. The old ones flake off, taking germs with them. Skin is also a little oily and a little sour, which many germs dislike. And it is covered in friendly microbes, which leave no room for germs. A cut is a hole in the wall. That is why we wash a cut with clean water and cover it.
examples: Germs land on your hands all day. They stay outside unless you have a cut, or you rub your eyes, nose or mouth.
A mosquito bite is a tiny hole. That is how the malaria germ gets past the skin.
Your skin makes a whole new top layer about every month or two. Some of the dust in a house is old skin flakes.
explanations.art: A side view of skin like stacked roof tiles, with the top tiles flaking off and carrying germs away, and new tiles forming below.
explanations.context: This card explains how your skin keeps germs out. It is the body's first wall.

explanations.concept: Wet walls: tears, mucus, spit and stomach acid
explanations.definition: Tears, mucus, saliva and stomach acid are wet walls. They wash germs away, trap them, or kill them before they can get inside the body.
explanations.description: Your eyes, nose and mouth are openings, so skin cannot cover them. Wet walls guard them instead. Tears wash your eyes every time you blink. The hairs just inside your nose catch bigger bits of dust. Sticky mucus traps smaller dust and germs. Further in, even tinier hairs called cilia sweep the mucus up to your throat, where you swallow it or cough it out. Saliva washes your mouth. Anything you swallow lands in stomach acid, a juice so sour that it kills many germs. Tears, mucus and saliva also hold a chemical called lysozyme. It cuts open the outer coat of some bacteria, so they burst.
examples: When you chop onions, your eyes stream with tears. They are washing out the stinging gas from the onion.
A sneeze blasts trapped dust and germs out of your nose.
In 1921 Alexander Fleming, a Scottish doctor, had a cold. A drop from his runny nose fell on a dish of bacteria, and the bacteria near it dissolved. That is how lysozyme was found.
explanations.art: A face with three labels: tears washing the eye, a sticky nose with tiny hairs, and spit in the mouth, with an arrow down to a bubbling stomach.
explanations.context: This card explains the wet walls at your eyes, nose and mouth, which trap and kill germs.

explanations.concept: White blood cells: the defenders inside
explanations.definition: White blood cells are cells that travel in the blood, find germs and destroy them. Some eat germs whole. Others make chemicals that stick to germs, or remember them.
explanations.description: Your blood is mostly red blood cells, which carry oxygen, the part of the air your body needs. Mixed in with them are a few white blood cells. There is only about one white cell for every 700 red ones. White blood cells are made inside your bones, in a soft middle part called bone marrow. They ride around in the blood. When germs get in, the hurt cells send out chemical signals, like a smell. White blood cells follow the smell. A blood vessel is a tube that blood flows in. White blood cells squeeze out through its wall and crawl to the germs. Some kinds, called phagocytes, wrap around a germ and eat them. Other kinds make sticky chemicals that grab germs, or remember a germ for next time. You will learn about those in a later unit.
examples: In a cut finger, white blood cells arrive within an hour or so.
White blood cells are not really white. Each one is almost see-through. A big pile of them looks pale and creamy.
Your body makes billions of new white blood cells every day, because many of them only live for a few days.
explanations.art: A blood vessel drawn like a road, with red cells like discs and one round white cell squeezing out through a gap in the wall towards a germ.
explanations.context: This card explains white blood cells: the tiny cells in your blood that hunt and eat germs.

explanations.concept: Red, warm, swollen and sore: inflammation
explanations.definition: Inflammation is when part of the body goes red, warm, swollen and sore because extra blood is bringing white blood cells there to fight.
explanations.description: When germs get into a cut, the cells nearby call for help. The tiny blood vessels there get wider and a little leaky. More blood comes, so the skin goes red and warm. Some water leaks out, so it swells up. The swelling presses on nerves, so it feels sore. All of this lets white blood cells pour into the spot. This fight is called inflammation. About two thousand years ago, a Roman writer called Celsus listed its four signs: redness, heat, swelling and pain. When white blood cells die fighting, they pile up with dead germs. That pale goo is pus. A scab forms on top, like a lid, while new skin grows underneath.
examples: A splinter in your finger: the skin round it goes pink and puffy within a day.
A mosquito bite goes red and itchy. That is your body reacting to the mosquito's spit.
A pimple's white tip is pus, left over from a small fight against germs.
explanations.art: Four little pictures of a finger with a splinter: red, warm (wavy lines), swollen, and a small 'ouch' face.
explanations.context: This card explains why a cut goes red, warm and puffy. It is a sign that your body is fighting there.

explanations.concept: Fever: the body turns up the heat
explanations.definition: A fever is when the brain sets the body's heat higher than usual, often because the immune system is fighting germs.
explanations.description: Your body keeps itself at about 37 degrees Celsius, whether the day is hot or cold. A part of your brain works like the knob on an iron. It sets how hot you should be. When white blood cells meet germs, they send chemicals to the brain. The brain turns the knob up. Now 37 degrees feels too cold, so you shiver and want a blanket, until you warm up. That is a fever. Many germs grow more slowly when it is hotter. And some white blood cells work faster. When the fight is over, the brain turns the knob back down. Then you feel too hot, and you sweat until you cool off.
examples: Doctors usually call 38 degrees Celsius or more a fever. That is 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit.
At the start of a fever you may shiver, even though your forehead feels hot.
When a fever breaks, you often wake up sweaty.
explanations.art: A brain with a dial like an iron's heat knob, turned from 37 to 38.5 degrees, and a shivering child pulling up a blanket.
explanations.context: This card explains what a fever is and why it happens.

explanations.concept: When a fever needs a doctor
explanations.definition: Most fevers need rest, water and a watchful grown-up. Some warning signs mean a doctor should see the child quickly.
explanations.description: Most fevers in children are the body doing its job, and they pass in two or three days. A grown-up gives plenty of water and lets the child rest. If the child feels very uncomfortable, a grown-up can ask a doctor what to do. Children never take medicine by themselves. Some fevers need a doctor quickly. A grown-up should call a doctor for any fever in a baby under 3 months old. They should also call if a fever reaches 40 degrees Celsius or lasts more than 3 days. Call at once if the fever comes with a stiff neck, a new rash, trouble breathing or a fit. Call at once, too, if the child is very hard to wake.
examples: A child has a fever of 38.4 degrees and a runny nose, but still plays a little. Rest, water and watching are enough.
A child has a fever with a stiff neck and a rash. A doctor must see them at once.
Feeling hot is not enough to know. A thermometer tells you the real number.
explanations.art: A simple card a parent could stick on the fridge: a thermometer, a water glass and a bed on one side, and a doctor's bag with the warning signs on the other.
explanations.context: This card is for the family. It says what to do when someone has a fever, and when to call a doctor.

explanations.concept: Should we bring a fever down?
explanations.description: Since fever helps fight germs, should we stop it? People have argued about this for a long time. Today doctors mostly agree on what to do, but scientists still study why.
examples: Some families give a fever medicine so a child can sleep. Others wait. Doctors say a fever medicine is for comfort, and a doctor should say which one and how much.
Scientists have tested fever medicines in many sick children. Most studies found the medicines did not make illnesses last much longer.

perspectives.who: Many doctors long ago, and many families today
perspectives.explanation: The fever is the danger, so it must be brought down fast. Some people even wake a sleeping child to give medicine, or sponge them with cold water.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study fever in animals, such as Matthew Kluger in the 1970s
perspectives.explanation: Fever is an old, useful defence. Sick lizards that were kept cool were more likely to die than lizards allowed to warm up. So fever helps, and we should not be afraid of it.

perspectives.who: Children's doctors today, for example the American Academy of Pediatrics and the UK's NHS
perspectives.explanation: Treat the child, not the number. A fever medicine is for comfort, not to reach a 'normal' number. Watch the child, and see a doctor if there are warning signs.

explanations.art: Two scales: on one side a child sleeping comfortably, on the other side a thermometer and germs, with a question mark between.
explanations.context: This card is about a question doctors and scientists have argued over: is it good or bad to bring a fever down?

explanations.concept: How does the body tell 'me' from 'not me'?
explanations.description: White blood cells leave your own cells alone, but they attack germs. How do they know the difference? This is one of the biggest questions in the study of the immune system. Scientists have given different answers, and the story is still being worked out.
examples: Your immune system does not attack the food you eat, though food is from outside.
It leaves alone the billions of friendly microbes in your gut.
A mother's body does not attack the baby growing inside her, though half of the baby's genes come from the father.

perspectives.who: Frank Macfarlane Burnet, an Australian scientist, around 1949 to 1959
perspectives.explanation: While a baby is growing, the body learns what 'self' is. Later, anything that is not self gets attacked. He shared a Nobel Prize for this work in 1960.

perspectives.who: Polly Matzinger, an American scientist, in 1994
perspectives.explanation: The body does not attack things just because they are new. It attacks when cells send 'danger' signals, like hurt cells do. That is why it leaves food and friendly microbes alone. She came to science late, after working as a jazz musician, a carpenter and a dog trainer. At first many scientists disagreed with her.
Both ideas are partly right. The body does learn its own self. It also listens for danger signals. Exactly how these work together is still being studied.

explanations.art: A white blood cell at a crossroads: one road leads to the body's own cells with a green tick, another to a germ with a red cross, and a third to a bowl of rice with a question mark.
explanations.context: This card is about a big question: how the immune system knows what belongs to you and what does not.

explanations.concept: Friendly microbes are part of the defence
explanations.definition: The microbiome is all the microbes that live on and in you. Many of them help protect you by leaving no room or food for germs.
explanations.description: You are never alone. About as many bacteria live on and in your body as there are cells of your own. Scientists counted in 2016 and found roughly 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells in a grown-up. Almost all of them are harmless or helpful. On your skin and in your gut they eat the food that germs want, and take up the space that germs want. Some even make chemicals that keep germs away. So washing with soap is good, but scrubbing your skin raw is not. Your friendly microbes are part of your wall.
examples: A healthy gut is packed with friendly bacteria, so germs struggle to settle there.
Curd and idli batter are full of friendly microbes.
Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria. After taking them, some people get tummy trouble, because friendly gut bacteria were killed too.
explanations.art: A skin surface drawn like a crowded market of friendly microbes, with one germ looking for space and finding none.
explanations.context: This card explains that friendly microbes on and in your body help keep germs away.

explanations.definition: All living things, from bacteria to plants to people, have ways to keep out or fight what harms them.
explanations.description: The immune system is not only a human thing. Every living thing has some way to keep out what harms them. Plants have no blood and no white blood cells. But their leaves have waxy coats, and they can close the tiny holes in their leaves when germs land. A hurt plant makes sticky sap and sends chemical alarms to their other leaves. Even bacteria, which are single cells, have a way to cut up viruses that attack them, and to remember them. Scientists found this in bacteria used to make curd and yoghurt. Insects, fish and lizards fight germs too. Some of them warm up on purpose when they are sick.
examples: A neem or mango tree oozes sticky gum where their bark is hurt. The gum seals the wound.
Sick lizards in a lab moved to the warmest spot they could find, giving themselves a fever.
Honeybees heat up their hive when a harmful fungus attacks the baby bees.
explanations.art: A row: a leaf closing its tiny pores, a tree trunk with sticky gum, a single bacterium cutting a virus, and a lizard basking on a warm rock.
explanations.context: This card shows that plants, insects, lizards and even bacteria defend themselves against germs, each in their own way.

explanations.concept: Down to the molecules: shapes that fit
explanations.definition: Immune cells and chemicals recognise germs by touch. Their molecules fit the molecules on the germ, and tiny electric forces of attraction hold them together.
explanations.description: A white blood cell has no eyes. The cell finds out what a germ is by touch. The outside of every cell, and every germ, is covered in molecules. A molecule is a tiny group of atoms joined together, and each kind has its own shape. A white blood cell has their own molecules on their outside, called receptors. When a receptor fits a molecule on a germ, like a key in a lock, the cell grabs on. Tiny electric forces between the atoms attract each other and hold the two together. That is how the cell knows to attack. Lysozyme, the chemical in your tears, works the same way. Its shape fits a part of a germ's coat, and it snips it.
examples: A white blood cell bumps into thousands of things. They grab only those whose shapes fit their receptors.
Lysozyme is also found in egg white. An enzyme is a chemical that does a job in living things. In 1965, lysozyme became the first enzyme whose full shape scientists worked out, using X-rays.
explanations.art: A big zoom: a white blood cell's surface with tiny lock shapes, and a germ's surface with matching key shapes clicking into one.
explanations.context: This card zooms all the way in, to the tiny shapes that let white blood cells recognise germs.

explanations.concept: Sleep, food, play and the immune system
explanations.definition: Good sleep, varied food, daily play, handwashing and vaccines all help the immune system. No single food or drink 'boosts' it.
explanations.description: There is no magic food or drink that 'boosts' your immune system. But the whole body works better when it is looked after, and the immune system is part of the body. Doctors agree on a few simple things. Sleep well, because the body does a lot of repair at night. Eat many kinds of food, including vegetables, fruit, dal and grains. Play and move every day. Wash your hands with soap before eating and after the toilet, so fewer germs reach your mouth. Get the vaccines your doctor offers. A vaccine shows your immune system a harmless form of a germ, so it can fight the real germ quickly.
examples: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night.
Washing hands with soap and water for about 20 seconds removes many more germs than water alone.
Adverts often say a drink 'boosts immunity'. That is usually not what scientists have found.
explanations.art: A day in four small pictures: a child sleeping, eating a thali with many colours, running outside, and washing hands with soap.
explanations.context: This card is about everyday habits that help the immune system do its job.

explanations.description: Scientists have learnt a huge amount about the immune system. But some big puzzles are still open. Why do two people catch the same germ, and one gets very ill while the other hardly notices? When we are ill, we feel tired, grumpy and sleepy. How exactly does the immune system send these signals to the brain? Why do some immune systems attack harmless things like pollen or peanuts? There are ideas about all of these, but no full answers yet.
examples: Feeling sleepy and sad when ill seems to be partly caused by chemicals from white blood cells reaching the brain. Scientists think this makes us rest.
The same cold virus can give one child a sniffle and another child a fever.
explanations.art: A scientist at a microscope surrounded by floating question marks shaped like cells.
explanations.context: This card lists some big questions about the immune system that scientists have not yet answered.

agreed.text: Germs cause many illnesses, and most of them must get past the skin or the wet walls to make us ill.
agreed.evidence: In the 1870s and 1880s, Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch showed that particular germs cause particular diseases. Koch grew the germs of anthrax and tuberculosis from sick animals and people. Washing hands and cleaning wounds cuts infections a lot.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: germs cause illness.

agreed.text: White blood cells find and destroy germs.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, scientists have filmed white blood cells chasing and swallowing bacteria. In 1882, Élie Metchnikoff saw cells like these gather round a thorn.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: white blood cells fight germs.

agreed.text: Redness, warmth, swelling and pus are signs that the body is fighting, not just signs of damage.
agreed.evidence: When scientists look at swollen tissue under a microscope, it is full of white blood cells that have come out of the blood.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: why a cut goes red and puffy.

agreed.text: A fever is controlled by the brain, and it usually helps the body fight germs.
agreed.evidence: Chemicals made by white blood cells reach the brain and raise the body's set heat. In many animals, sick ones that can warm up survive better.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: fevers.

agreed.text: Most microbes are harmless or helpful, and many live on and in us.
agreed.evidence: When scientists count and name the microbes on skin and in the gut, almost all are harmless. Some help digest food or keep germs away.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: most microbes are not germs.

agreed.text: All living things, even a single bacterium, have some way to defend themselves.
agreed.evidence: Plants close leaf pores and send chemical alarms. In 2007, scientists showed that bacteria cut up viruses with a system called CRISPR.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: all life defends itself.

agreed.text: Vaccines protect people from serious illnesses caused by germs.
agreed.evidence: After years of vaccination all over the world, smallpox disappeared. Its last natural case was in 1977. India has had no new case of wild polio since 2011, after millions of children were given polio drops.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: vaccines protect people.

challenging.claim: All germs are bad, and the cleaner everything is, the better.
challenging.who: Many adverts for cleaning products, and many of us without noticing.
challenging.for: Some germs really do cause serious illness. Washing hands with soap really does stop many of them spreading.
challenging.against: Only a few microbes are germs. Friendly microbes on our skin and in our gut help guard us. Scientists think that meeting many harmless microbes when young, outdoors and with animals, may help the immune system learn. Scrubbing everything with strong chemicals is not needed.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea, that all germs are bad, and why scientists disagree with it.

challenging.claim: Illness comes from bad air, or 'miasma', not from tiny living things.
challenging.who: Many doctors in Europe and India until the late 1800s.
challenging.for: Diseases like cholera were common near stinking drains and dirty water. Cleaning up drains really did reduce illness.
challenging.against: Germs were found in the 1800s. Cholera spreads through dirty water carrying a germ, not through the smell itself. Cleaning drains helped because it removed the germs.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where illness comes from, and why it was given up.

challenging.claim: A fever is dangerous in itself, so it must always be brought down quickly.
challenging.who: Many families, and many doctors in the past.
challenging.for: A very high fever can be a sign of serious illness, and fever makes children feel awful.
challenging.against: In most children a fever is the body fighting, and it does no harm by itself. Doctors today say to treat the child's comfort and watch for warning signs, rather than chase a number.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that every fever is dangerous.

challenging.claim: The immune system attacks only things that send danger signals, not simply anything foreign.
challenging.who: Polly Matzinger, an American immunologist, in 1994. Her 'danger model'.
challenging.for: The body leaves food, friendly microbes and a growing baby alone, though they are all 'not self'.
challenging.against: The body really does learn its own self, and some foreign things are attacked even without much harm. Most scientists now think both self and danger matter.
challenging.context: This card is about a challenging idea of how the immune system decides what to attack.

challenging.claim: Germs inside the body are killed only by chemicals in the blood, not by cells that eat them.
challenging.who: Paul Ehrlich and many other scientists, from the 1880s. Élie Metchnikoff said cells did the work. They argued for about 25 years.
challenging.for: Each side had strong experiments. Metchnikoff watched cells eat. Ehrlich and others showed blood without cells could still kill some germs.
challenging.against: Both were right. In 1908 they shared the Nobel Prize. The immune system uses both eating cells and germ-grabbing chemicals.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous argument between two scientists about how the body fights germs, and how it ended.

challenging.claim: You catch a cold just from being cold or getting your hair wet.
challenging.who: Many grandparents, and many of us.
challenging.for: Colds are more common in the cold months. Some studies suggest that cold noses may fight viruses a little less well.
challenging.against: A cold is caused by a virus. Without the virus, you cannot catch a cold however cold you get. In winter people also crowd indoors, which helps viruses spread.
challenging.context: This card is about the common belief that getting cold gives you a cold.

big_questions.q: If more than half the living cells on and in you are microbes, which part is really 'you'?
big_questions.hint: Your friendly microbes help guard you and digest your food. Are they visitors, or part of you?

big_questions.q: Your white blood cells fight for you every second, but you never notice them. What else is your body doing right now without asking you?
big_questions.hint: Think about your heart, your breathing and your blinking.

big_questions.q: A white blood cell dies fighting a germ, and becomes pus. Is that sad, brave, or just what cells do?
big_questions.hint: Think of people who protect others, like firefighters or nurses.

big_questions.q: Why might it be good, not bad, that a cut goes red and sore?
big_questions.hint: What would happen if you never felt it, and never noticed the cut?

big_questions.q: Your skin keeps germs out, but it lets sweat out. What else must the body's walls let through?
big_questions.hint: Think about your nose and mouth. What must come in through them every minute?

big_questions.q: Why does a fever make you feel cold at first, when your body is getting hotter?
big_questions.hint: Think of the brain's heat knob being turned up. What does 37 degrees feel like then?

big_questions.q: Plants and even bacteria defend themselves. Does that mean they, in some way, know what they are?
big_questions.hint: A bacterium has no brain. But they can tell their own self from a virus.

big_questions.q: If germs are living things too, is it fair that we kill them?
big_questions.hint: Germs are not bad on purpose. They are trying to live, like us.

story.title: The Thorns of Messina
story.note: Élie Metchnikoff, the starfish larvae, the rose thorns and the family's trip to the circus in Messina, Sicily, in 1882 are real. He told the story himself, and his wife Olga wrote it down in her book about his life. Olga telling the story, her little brother Sasha, his splinter and all the talk are made up.
text: My name is Olga. In the winter of 1882 I lived in a white house above the sea, in a town called Messina, on the island of Sicily. My husband was Élie Metchnikoff. He studied animals so small and so clear that you could see right through them.

Our sitting room was not like other sitting rooms. There were glass dishes on every table. In every dish swam tiny baby starfish, each one smaller than a grain of rice. They were not star-shaped yet. They looked like little bells made of water. Élie would sit for hours with his eye pressed to a microscope, a tube of glass that makes small things look big.

"Come and look, Olga," he would say. And I would look. Inside each baby starfish, you could see everything. Their tiny stomach. Its thin walls. And something else. Small round blobs that drifted about inside them, all by themselves, like boats with no oars.
"What are they?" I asked.
"I do not know," said Élie. "They wander. Nobody has told them where to go. And yet they go."
My little brother Sasha was staying with us that winter. He was eight. He did not care for starfish. He cared for oranges, and for climbing the low wall at the end of the garden, and for the circus.
The circus had come to Messina, with performing monkeys and a man who ate fire. On a bright December afternoon, the whole family put on our good coats to go and see it. Everyone except Élie.
"Go," he said, waving his hand without looking up. "I will stay with my bells."
So we went. Sasha laughed until he hiccuped. But when we came home, Élie was standing in the middle of the sitting room. His hair was wild. His eyes were shining.
"Olga," he said. "I have had an idea. It may be the most important idea of my life."

This is what had happened. Alone in the quiet house, he had been watching the wandering blobs. And a thought had struck him, the way lightning strikes a tree. What if the blobs were guards? What if, when something got inside the starfish that should not be there, they came to fight it?
"But how can you know?" I said.
"I can test it," said Élie. "I can put something into a starfish, and see if the blobs come."

A few days before, we had made a Christmas tree for the children out of a small tangerine tree in the garden. Roses grew beside the tree. While we were at the circus, Élie had gone out into the garden and snapped off a few rose thorns.

That evening, very gently, he pushed a single rose thorn into each baby starfish. Then he covered the dishes and went to bed. He did not sleep. I heard him get up twice in the night, and stand by the dishes, and sit down again.

In the morning, Sasha woke with a cry. While climbing the garden wall the day before, he had pushed a splinter of wood into his finger. Now the finger was red and fat and hot. He held it up to me, frightened.
"It is getting worse," he said. "Look! The splinter is eating me."
Before I could answer, Élie called from the sitting room. His voice was strange, high and shaking.
"Olga! Come! Bring the boy!"

We ran in. Élie stood back from the microscope so I could look. There was the baby starfish, clear as a raindrop. There was the rose thorn, dark and sharp inside them. And all around the thorn, crowded together like people around a fire, were the wandering blobs. Hundreds of them. They had come from every part of the tiny body. They were pressing against the thorn. Some had wrapped themselves around its tip.
"They came," Élie whispered. "In the night, they all came."
Sasha pushed in to look. He squinted down the tube for a long time. Then he lifted his head and stared at his own red finger.
"Is that," he said slowly, "what is happening in me?"
I knelt down and took my brother's hand very gently. I looked at the red, fat finger, and then back at the dish. All at once I understood what Élie had found.

"Yes," I said. "I think it is. This redness is not the splinter eating you, Sasha. It is you. Your own blood is rushing here, carrying your own guards. That warmth is the fire they are standing round. The swelling is the crowd. The splinter got through your wall, and your body has sent an army to the spot where it broke in."
Sasha looked at his finger as if he had never seen it before. "So it is not getting worse?"
"It is getting busier," I said. "That is different." Behind me, Élie nodded, and he was smiling.
I took a needle and cleaned it in a flame, and I eased the splinter out. A tiny bead of yellow came after it. Sasha made a face. "What is that?"

"Those are guards that fought," I said quietly. "Some of them did not survive. They gave themselves up to keep you well." Élie was silent for a moment. Then he said, "Every one of us is defended like this. Every second. And nobody notices."

Within two days, Sasha's finger was pink and ordinary again. Over the next few years, Élie watched the same kind of guards in water fleas and in many other animals. He saw them swallow germs whole. The cells were given a name made from old Greek words. Phagocytes. The eating cells.

Many great scientists disagreed with him. Germs are killed by chemicals in the blood, they said. Not by little wandering blobs. The argument went on for twenty-five years. Then, in 1908, Élie was given the Nobel Prize, the biggest prize in science. He shared it with Paul Ehrlich, who had studied the chemicals in the blood. They had both been right. The body uses chemicals and cells together.

But the evening I remember best is not the evening of the prize. It is the evening of the circus, when we came home laughing and found him in the middle of the room with his hair on end. The monkeys and the fire-eater had been wonderful. But the real show had been in a glass dish, in a creature smaller than a grain of rice, where a crowd of tiny guards had gathered, in the dark, around a thorn from a Christmas rose.
story.epiphany: For the parent: redness, warmth and swelling around a cut feel like damage, but they are mostly the body's own response. Blood vessels widen and leak a little so that white blood cells, the eating cells Metchnikoff found, can crowd to the spot. Pus is the remains of that fight. The story's turn is Sasha seeing his own sore finger as a busy battlefield rather than a wound getting worse. It also quietly shows how a new idea can be doubted for years, and how two rivals can both be right.
ask: In the story, Sasha thought the splinter was eating him. What was really making his finger red and hot?
Why did Élie push thorns into the baby starfish? What did he think would happen?
What is the yellow bead that came out after the splinter?
Élie stayed home from the circus. Was that a good choice? Why do you think so?
Other scientists disagreed with Élie's idea for years. Why do you think new ideas are often doubted at first?

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Germ player: germs that got inside ____

rules: Cut out the germ cards and the defence cards. Keep them in two piles.
One player is the Germ. The other players are the Body. Each Body player holds 4 defence cards.
The Germ turns over a germ card and reads it out loud.
A Body player must play one defence card that stops this germ, and say how it works. For example, 'Stomach acid kills the germs on the guava.'
If the defence fits, the germ is stopped. Put both cards aside. The Body scores a point, and that player takes a new defence card from the pile.
If no one can stop them with a wall, the germ gets inside. Then only a WHITE BLOOD CELL, INFLAMMATION or FEVER card can stop them.
After 8 germ cards, swap sides. The side that stops the most germs wins.

check.q: Someone eats a guava without washing it. Which defence kills most of the germs on it?
options: Tears
Stomach acid
Nose hairs
check.why: Food goes down into the stomach, where a strong, sour acid kills most germs. Tears protect the eyes and nose hairs protect the nose, so they never meet the guava. A Body player who picks tears is thinking 'any defence works'. In this game, the defence must be in the right place.

flow.parent: Listen for the reason, not just the card. 'Skin stops it because it is a tight wall with no holes' is a great answer. If a cut or a mosquito is involved, the skin wall is broken, so the germ goes INSIDE.

check.q: The germ card says 'Germs in a cut that nobody washed.' The skin is broken. Which defence card can stop these germs now?
options: Tears
White blood cell
Saliva
check.why: Once germs are inside a cut, the outer walls are behind them. Now the inside defenders take over: white blood cells come through the blood and eat the germs. Tears and saliva only work at the eyes and mouth. Picking them is a sign of thinking every defence works everywhere.

flow.context: This is step 4 of 5 of Get Past the Walls! This is a card game about the body's defences. One side plays germs trying to get in. The other side plays the walls and white blood cells that stop them.

flow.do: Count the stopped germs on the score sheet.
flow.say: Let's count. Which defence did we use most? Which defences stopped germs that were already inside?
flow.kid: Count the germs you stopped. Which defence did you use most?
flow.think: Your real body plays this game every second, and it usually wins. What do you think happens on the days it doesn't?
flow.context: This is the last step of Get Past the Walls! This is a card game about the body's defences. One side plays germs trying to get in. The other side plays the walls and white blood cells that stop them.

worksheets.title: Body Defenders (core)

items.p: Germs land on your hands all day long. Yet most days you do not fall ill. What is the best reason?
opts: Germs are too small to hurt anyone
Your skin is a tight wall with no gaps, so most germs stay outside
Germs that land on hands always die at once
items.why: Skin is the body's biggest wall. Its top layer is made of flat dead cells packed tightly together, so germs cannot get through unless there is a cut. Germs are small, but some can make you very ill if they get inside. A strong answer names the skin as a wall.

items.p: Sort these. Is it a WALL that keeps germs out, or a defence INSIDE the body that fights germs that got in?
items.a: see items
items.why: Walls stop germs at the doors: skin, tears, mucus and stomach acid. Once germs are inside, white blood cells fight them, and a fever helps the fight.

items.p: Find the mistake. Divya, a girl in Class 3, says, 'Tears are only for when you are sad.' Use the onion activity and your blink count to show what is wrong.
items.a: Divya is wrong. When the onion was cut, my eyes made tears even though I was not sad. The tears washed out the stinging gas. And we blink about 15 times a minute, all day. Each blink spreads a thin layer of tears to wash and wet the eye.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence the child saw: tears came with the onion, without any sadness, and blinking spreads tears all day. It ends with the job of tears: to wash dust and germs out of the eyes.

items.p: Remember the Apple Skin Test? Apple A was left whole. Apple B had one clean cut. Which apple went soft and brown first, and why?
opts: Apple A, because whole apples rot from the inside
Both at the same time, because they are the same kind of apple
Apple B, because microbes got in through the cut
items.why: Microbes landed on both apples. On apple A, the skin kept them out. On apple B, the cut was an open door. A strong answer gives the reason, not just the letter: the skin is the wall, and a cut is a hole in it.

items.p: Each wall stops germs in its own way. Match each wall to how it works.
pairs: a tight cover of dead cells with no gaps
a sticky trap that catches dust and germs in the nose
wash dust and germs out of the eyes
kills many germs that come in with food
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each wall guards a different door. The skin covers everything. Mucus traps, tears wash, and the acid in the stomach kills many germs that get swallowed.

items.p: When germs get past the walls, ____ blood cells find them and eat them.
items.why: White blood cells travel in the blood and hunt germs. They are almost see-through, but a big crowd of them looks pale and creamy, like pus.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 4, scraped her knee. The next morning, the skin round the scrape is red, warm and puffy. What is most likely happening?
opts: The scrape is spreading and getting worse
Extra blood is bringing white blood cells to fight germs at the scrape
The skin round the scrape is dying
items.why: Redness, warmth and swelling are called inflammation. Blood vessels near the scrape widen, so more blood and more white blood cells reach the spot. It looks like damage, but it is the body at work. If the redness keeps spreading for days, or red lines appear, a grown-up should take her to a doctor.

items.p: Pus coming out of a cut means the germs are winning.
items.why: False. Many people believe this. Pus is mostly white blood cells that died fighting, with broken germs. So pus shows that the defenders have been working there. A cut with lots of pus, or one that gets more painful, still needs a doctor.

items.p: You get a cut on your finger. Put these in order, from first to last.
items: White blood cells eat the germs
A scab forms and new skin grows
items.a: order shown
items.why: First the wall breaks and germs get in. Then the defenders arrive through the blood and eat them. Last, the hole is sealed and new skin grows.

items.p: Which of these temperatures is a fever?
opts: 36.6 degrees Celsius
37.0 degrees Celsius
38.4 degrees Celsius
items.why: Doctors usually call 38 degrees Celsius or more a fever. 36.6 and 37 are both normal. Picking 37 often comes from thinking that anything above 36 is too hot.

items.p: A friend says, 'Germs can only get inside you through a cut.' Name two other doors into the body that germs can use. Say which wall guards each one.
items.a: The eyes are a door, and tears guard them. The nose is a door, and mucus and nose hairs guard it. The mouth is a door, and saliva and stomach acid guard it.
items.why: A strong answer names two real doors (eyes, nose, mouth) and the right wall for each. This is why we wash our hands before touching our face or eating.

items.p: Draw a scraped knee as if it were cut in half, seen from the side. Show the skin, a blood vessel, white blood cells, pus and a scab. Label each one.
items.a: A side view with the skin on top and a gap where it was scraped. A blood vessel runs below. White blood cells are coming out of the vessel towards the gap. Pus sits in the gap, and a scab covers the top.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the white blood cells coming from the blood, not from the air. It puts the scab on top, sealing the hole in the skin wall.

items.p: A family argues about whether children should play in mud.

views.says: Mud is full of germs. Keep the children clean and indoors.
Most microbes in mud are harmless. Children who meet lots of harmless microbes may get fewer allergies.
Mud play is fine. But wash hands before eating, and wash and cover any cut.

items.ask: Whose side are you on? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses the unit: for example, most microbes are harmless or helpful, or a cut is an open door for germs. Then it fairly gives another person's best point, for example that dirty hands carry germs into the mouth.
items.why: There is no single winner. Paati is right that some germs live in soil, as apple C showed. Amma's idea about allergies is studied by scientists, but it is not settled. Dr Revathi joins both: play, then wash.

items.p: Most microbes are harmless or helpful.
items.why: True. Only a few microbes are germs that make us ill. Many, like those in curd and on our skin, help us.

items.p: In the Sticky Nose Test, the sticky card caught many more dust specks than the smooth card. Which part of your nose works like the sticky card?
opts: The mucus
The bone in your nose
The nostril holes
items.why: Mucus is sticky, like the tape facing up. Dust and germs that touch it get stuck. Then you blow them out or swallow them, and stomach acid kills many of the swallowed germs.

items.p: A healthy body stays at about ____ degrees Celsius.
items.why: About 37 degrees Celsius. It changes a little through the day. Many home thermometers in India show Fahrenheit, where normal is about 98.6 degrees. Do not mix up the two scales.

worksheets.context: This worksheet checks the main ideas: the body's walls, white blood cells, inflammation, fever and friendly microbes.

worksheets.title: How the Defenders Work (stretch)

items.p: Why do you shiver at the start of a fever, even though you are getting hotter?
opts: Because the room is cold
Because germs are cold
The brain has turned the body's heat knob up, so normal now feels too cold
Because white blood cells are cold
items.why: In a fever the brain sets a new, higher temperature. Until the body reaches it, normal 37 degrees feels too cold, so you shiver and want a blanket. Shivering makes heat. Picking 'the room is cold' is natural, but you shiver even in a warm room.

items.p: Dust tickles the inside of your nose, and you sneeze. What is the sneeze doing for you?
opts: Pulling more dust deep into your chest
Blowing the dust and germs, caught in mucus, out of your nose
Warming up your nose
items.why: A sneeze is the nose's wall at work. The mucus catches dust and germs, and the sneeze blasts them out. A strong answer says what is thrown out and why it helps.

items.p: Remember the four apples? Apple C had soil rubbed into its cut. Apple D had soil rubbed in too, and then was washed. Apple C went bad faster. What does this tell you about what to do with a scrape?
items.a: Soil has many microbes, and some of them rot apples or cause illness. Washing took many of them away, so apple D rotted more slowly. So when I scrape my knee, I should wash it with clean water, and then cover it.
items.why: A strong answer says what the apples showed, and then uses it for a new case: a scrape. It names washing as the thing that made the difference.

items.p: Lalitha, a girl in Class 4, has a fever of 38.5 degrees Celsius. She feels tired but is drinking water. Three people give different advice.

views.says: Give her fever medicine now. A high number is dangerous, so bring it down fast.
Let the fever be. The body turned up the heat to fight the germs.
Watch the child, not the number. Give medicine if she is uncomfortable or cannot sleep. Call me if there are warning signs.

items.ask: Whose advice would you follow? Use what you know about fever. Then say one thing another person gets right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the science: a fever is the brain turning up the heat, many germs grow more slowly in the heat, and sick lizards kept cool were more likely to die. It then admits another fair point, for example that medicine can help a child sleep and drink, or that some fevers need a doctor.
items.why: This is a real argument. Doctors today mostly agree with Dr Meera: medicine is for comfort, and warning signs matter more than the number. The grandmother is right that fever helps. The aunt is right that a child who is very unwell needs care.

items.p: Predict. A girl blinks about 15 times a minute while she chats. While she reads an exciting book, she blinks only about 5 times a minute. After an hour of reading, how might her eyes feel? Why?
items.a: Her eyes might feel dry, tired or itchy. Each blink spreads tears over the eye to wet it and wash it. With fewer blinks, the eyes get less washing and dry out.
items.why: A strong answer links blinking to tears, and tears to the eye's wall. It might add a fix: look up from the book and blink now and then.

items.p: A white blood cell finds a germ by…
opts: Looking with tiny eyes
Following chemical signals and feeling the germ's shapes
Listening for them
Waiting for the germ to come to them
items.why: Hurt cells release chemicals, and white blood cells crawl towards them. When they touch a germ, shapes fit together like a key in a lock. White blood cells have no eyes or ears. Picking 'eyes' is natural, because that's how we find things.

items.p: A fever is always dangerous and must always be brought down quickly.
items.why: False. Most fevers are the body fighting germs, and they pass in a few days. Doctors say to look after the child's comfort and watch for warning signs, rather than chase a number.

items.p: Challenge the belief. A girl's grandmother says, 'You went out with wet hair, so you caught a cold.' The girl says, 'A cold is caused by a virus.' Who is right, and how could both be partly right?
items.a: The girl is right that a cold needs a virus. Without the virus, wet hair cannot give you a cold. But some studies suggest that a cold nose fights viruses a little less well. So getting chilly might help a virus that is already there.
items.why: A strong answer says what causes a cold (a virus) and then treats the grandmother's idea fairly. Scientists are still studying how cold weather affects colds.

items.p: Sort these. Does it HELP the immune system, or is it a MYTH?
items: scrubbing skin until it is raw
items.a: see items
items.why: Sleep, varied food, play and handwashing help the body work well. No single drink boosts immunity, and scrubbing skin raw damages the wall and its friendly microbes.

items.p: Remember the lizard's fever activity? In real experiments, sick lizards crawled to warmer places. Why?
opts: Because they were bored
Because they were hungry
To give themselves a fever, which helps them fight germs
Because cold makes germs grow
items.why: Lizards make very little heat of their own, so they use warm rocks. Sick lizards chose warmer spots, and those kept cool were more likely to die. Fever is an old defence. Picking 'cold makes germs grow' is not right: many germs grow more slowly in heat.

items.p: Why do doctors say to sneeze into your elbow, not your hand? Use your Sneeze Stopper test.
items.a: Both catch the drops. But my hand then touches food, faces and door handles, and passes the germs on. My elbow hardly touches anything.
items.why: A strong answer says that hands spread germs after the sneeze, and uses the spots on the paper from the Sneeze Stopper test as evidence that a sleeve catches drops.

items.p: Draw three pictures to show a phagocyte eating a germ: touch, wrap, swallow.
items.a: 1. A blob cell touching a small germ. 2. The cell's edges wrapping around the germ. 3. The germ inside the cell.
items.why: Phagocytes eat germs by wrapping around them and pulling them inside, where chemicals break them down.

items.p: A white blood cell that eats germs is called a ____. The word means 'eating cell'.
items.why: Phagocyte comes from old Greek words for eating and cell. Élie Metchnikoff studied these cells, starting with baby starfish in 1882.

items.p: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria. Shanthi, a girl in Class 4, has a cold, which is caused by a virus. Will an antibiotic help her get better?
opts: Yes, antibiotics kill every kind of germ
No. Antibiotics do not work on viruses. Rest, water and her own immune system will beat the cold.
Only if she takes a double dose
items.why: Many people think antibiotics cure colds. They do not, because a cold is caused by a virus, not bacteria. Taking antibiotics when they are not needed also helps bacteria learn to survive them. A strong answer says why: antibiotics work on bacteria only.

items.p: After a cut, you can see signs of the body's fight. Match each sign to what is causing it.
pairs: more blood flowing to the spot
fluid and white blood cells coming out of the blood vessels
white blood cells that fought, with dead germs
dried blood sealing the hole in the skin
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each sign has a cause inside the body. Together they show the steps: more blood comes, defenders leave the vessels, they fight, and the hole is sealed.

items.p: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form of a germ, such as a dead or weakened one. Why does this help when the real germ comes later?
opts: The body recognises the germ and fights them much faster
The vaccine makes the skin thicker
The vaccine kills every microbe in the body
items.why: The immune system remembers the shapes on a germ. After a vaccine, the body has met those shapes already. When the real germ arrives, the body is ready, and fights before the germ can make you very ill.

worksheets.context: This worksheet uses the ideas on new cases: fever advice, colds, antibiotics, vaccines and what the tests showed.

worksheets.title: Me, Not-Me and Every Living Thing (challenge)

items.p: Your immune system does not attack the food you eat, even though food comes from outside. What is one idea scientists have for why?
opts: Food has no shapes on it
The stomach hides food from white blood cells forever
It attacks only things that send 'danger' signals, like hurt cells
White blood cells are asleep after meals
items.why: Polly Matzinger's 'danger model' says the immune system reacts to danger, not just to anything new. Food, friendly microbes and a growing baby don't send danger signals. Most scientists think danger and 'self' both matter. Food does have shapes, so that answer doesn't work.

items.p: Plants have no blood and no white blood cells. How do they defend themselves?
opts: They can't defend themselves at all
Waxy leaves, closing leaf pores, sticky sap and chemical alarms
They run away from germs
They grow white blood cells in their roots
items.why: Plants have their own defences. They close the tiny holes in their leaves when germs land, seal wounds with sap, and send chemical warnings to other leaves. Picking 'can't defend' is natural, because we can't see a plant's fight.

items.p: Bacteria are single cells. Can they defend themselves against viruses?
opts: No, bacteria have no defences
Only if they live inside people
Yes, some cut up virus pieces and remember them, using a system called CRISPR
Only in hot places
items.why: In 2007, scientists found that some bacteria, like those used to make yoghurt, store bits of the viruses that attacked them. Next time, they use these bits to recognise the virus and cut them up. Even a single cell has an immune system.

items.p: A body thermometer reads 101 degrees Fahrenheit. What is that in Celsius, roughly, and is it a fever?
opts: About 101 degrees Celsius: boiling hot
About 38.3 degrees Celsius: yes, a fever
About 36 degrees Celsius: normal
You can't tell
items.why: Normal is about 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit, which is 37 degrees Celsius. A fever starts at about 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit, which is 38 degrees Celsius. So 101 Fahrenheit is about 38.3 Celsius, a fever. Picking 101 Celsius mixes up the two scales.
items.art: Two thermometer faces side by side, one in Celsius and one in Fahrenheit.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3, took her temperature four times in one day. It read 36.3 degrees Celsius at 7 am and 36.9 after running. What is the best explanation?
opts: Her body has a fever after running
Body temperature changes a little through the day, and moving muscles make heat
The thermometer is broken
items.why: A small change of half a degree or so is normal. Moving muscles make heat, and the body is coolest early in the morning. 36.9 is not a fever, because a fever is 38 or more.

chart.title: One child's temperature through a day (example numbers)

items.p: White blood cells sometimes attack the body's own cells by mistake.
items.why: True. This is called an autoimmune illness. It shows how hard the job of telling 'me' from 'not me' is. You will learn more in Class 5.

items.p: Put a fever in order, from start to finish.
items: White blood cells meet germs and send chemicals to the brain
The brain turns the heat knob up
You shiver and feel cold until you warm up
The germs are beaten and the knob turns down
items.a: order shown
items.why: The signal comes first, then the new setting, then shivering to reach it. When the fight ends, the setting drops, and you sweat to cool down.

items.p: Match each living thing to their defence.
pairs: sticky gum that seals a wound
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: All living things defend themselves, each in their own way.

items.p: Two real scientists argued for about 25 years about how the body kills germs that get inside.

views.who: Élie Metchnikoff, who studied baby starfish
views.says: Cells kill germs. I saw wandering cells crowd round a thorn and swallow germs.
Chemicals in the blood kill germs. Blood with no cells in it can still kill some bacteria.

items.ask: Which scientist would you have backed in 1890? Give your reason. Then say what the other one had right.
items.a: A strong answer backs one side with his own evidence: the crowd of cells round the thorn, or blood with no cells still killing bacteria. Then it says what the other got right. The best answers notice that both pieces of evidence were real, so both ideas could be true.
items.why: In 1908 they shared the Nobel Prize. The body uses both: cells that eat germs, and chemicals in the blood that grab them. Two people who disagree can each see part of the truth.

items.p: Some adverts say a drink 'boosts your immunity'. How could a scientist find out if that is true?
items.a: Take two groups of children who are alike. Give one group the drink and the other a pretend drink that looks the same. Nobody knows who got which. Count who gets ill more often over a few months.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing and counts the results. Pretend drinks help stop people's hopes from changing the results.

items.p: About half the living cells on and in your body are microbes, mostly in your gut. Two cousins argue about them.

views.says: My microbes are part of me. They help me digest food and keep germs away. I could not live well without them.
My microbes are not me. They are separate living beings who came from outside and could live somewhere else.

items.ask: Whose side are you on? Give a reason. Then say the best point the other cousin makes.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with a fact: friendly microbes help digest food and crowd out germs, or microbes are separate beings with their own DNA. Then it fairly states the other cousin's best point.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Scientists and philosophers argue about this too. The immune system itself has to decide, every day, which microbes belong.

items.p: Draw the body's defences as a castle, with walls, gates, guards and a heat knob. Label each one with the body part it stands for.
items.a: A castle with a skin wall, eye, nose and mouth gates with tears, mucus and saliva, white blood cell guards on a blood road, and a heat knob for fever, all labelled.
items.why: A model drawing like this shows how the defences work in layers.

items.p: What if your body could not make a fever at all? Predict what might happen when germs get in. Use the lizard experiment as evidence.
items.a: The germs might grow faster, because many germs grow more slowly when it is hotter. Some white blood cells also work faster when warm. The lizards kept cool were more likely to die, so without fever I might get more ill, or stay ill longer.
items.why: A strong answer gives a prediction and a reason, then uses the lizards as evidence. It might add that fever is not the only defence, so the walls and white blood cells would still help.

items.p: Find the mistake. An advert says, 'This cream kills 99.9% of germs on your skin. Use it every hour!' What is wrong with using it every hour?
items.a: Most microbes on the skin are harmless or helpful. They take up space and food, so harmful germs find it harder to settle. Killing them every hour harms the skin's helpers, and rubbing the skin again and again can dry and crack it, which opens doors for germs.
items.why: A strong answer uses two ideas from the unit: friendly microbes help guard the skin, and a cracked skin wall lets germs in. Washing hands with soap before eating is enough for most days.

items.p: Sometimes the immune system fights something harmless, like pollen or dust, as if it were a germ. This is called an ____.
items.why: An allergy is the defenders making a mistake: sneezing, itching or a rash against something that would never hurt you. Scientists still argue about why allergies have become more common.

items.p: Sort these. Do scientists agree on this, or do they still argue about it?
items: a cold is caused by a virus
skin keeps germs out unless it is broken
why allergies have become more common
exactly how the body tells harmless microbes from harmful ones
items.a: see items
items.why: Some things have been tested again and again. Others are still open. A strong answer can say why an open question is hard: there are trillions of microbes, and each person's body is a little different.

worksheets.context: This worksheet is for children who want a challenge: how the body tells self from not-self, defences in plants and bacteria, and open questions.

experiments.title: The Apple Skin Test
experiments.context: In this experiment you test four apples. One keeps its skin whole, and three get a small cut. You watch them for about a week to see which go bad first, and where the rot begins. It shows how skin keeps germs out.
experiments.question: Does unbroken skin keep germs out of an apple? What happens if the skin is cut, and what helps a cut?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which apple will go soft and bad first? Which will stay fresh longest? Why do you think so? Write your guess for each apple.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use four apples that are the same kind and look the same. Make each cut the same size, with the same clean knife. Keep all four bags in the same place. Only one thing changes: what happens to the skin.

materials.item: apples of the same kind, all fresh with no bruises
clean plastic bags: zip-lock bags, or bags from the vegetable shop tied in a knot
a small kitchen knife, used only by a grown-up
a spoonful of soil from a potted plant, or dust swept from a balcony
a clean cloth and a tap with running water
a marker pen and labels

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up uses the knife. Wash hands with soap after touching the soil. Never open the bags after day 1, because mould can grow inside. Throw the closed bags away at the end.

schedule.what: Guess. Label the apples. A grown-up makes the cuts. Rub soil on two cuts, and rinse one of them. Close the bags.
Look at each apple through the bag. Write what you see.
Look again and write what you see.
Look again and write what you see.
Last look. Compare the apples. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Each time you look, write one or two words for each apple: fresh, brown, soft patch, soft and wet, or mouldy. On day 7, draw each apple and show where the soft patch began.

setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts apples B, C and D. Apple A keeps its skin whole.

flow.do: Show your child the four apples. Ask them to guess which will go bad first and why.
flow.say: Here are four apples. An apple's skin is a bit like your skin. It is a wall. We are going to test what happens if the wall is broken. Which apple do you think will go bad first?
flow.kid: Look at the four apples. Their skin is like your skin. Guess which apple will go bad first. Write your guess.

good: The cut one with dirt, because germs can get in.
The whole one will stay fresh, because the skin keeps germs out.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Apple Skin Test. In this experiment you test four apples. One has its skin whole, and three have a small cut. You watch them for about a week to see which go bad first. It shows how skin keeps germs out.

flow.do: 1. Label the apples A, B, C and D. 2. Leave A whole. 3. Make one cut about 2 centimetres long in B, C and D, all the same size.
flow.say: Apple A keeps its skin whole. I will make a small cut in B, C and D. Watch: I make each cut the same size, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts apples B, C and D. Apple A stays whole. Each cut is the same size.
flow.parent: Use a clean knife and wipe it between apples. Cuts about 2 cm long and shallow are enough.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 6 of The Apple Skin Test. In this experiment you test four apples. One has its skin whole, and three have a small cut. You watch them for about a week to see which go bad first. It shows how skin keeps germs out.

flow.do: 1. Rub a little soil into the cuts on C and D with a finger. 2. Rinse cut D under running tap water for 10 seconds, then pat it dry with a clean cloth. 3. Wash hands with soap. 4. Put each apple in its own bag, close it and label it.
flow.say: Soil has lots of microbes in it, and some are the kind that make fruit rot. C gets soil and stays dirty. D gets soil, then we wash it, like you would wash a scraped knee. B is cut but clean.
flow.kid: Rub a little soil on cuts C and D. Rinse cut D under the tap. Wash your hands with soap. Put each apple in its own bag.

check.q: In the apple skin test, why do we wash cut D but not cut C?
options: To see if washing a cut helps
To make apple D taste better
Because D was the biggest cut
check.why: C and D both get soil. The only difference is washing. So if D stays fresher than C, washing must be what helped. That is a fair test: only one thing changes. Picking 'biggest cut' would break the fair test, because all the cuts are the same size.

flow.context: This is step 3 of 6 of The Apple Skin Test. In this experiment you test four apples. One has its skin whole, and three have a small cut. You watch them for about a week to see which go bad first. It shows how skin keeps germs out.

flow.do: Look at the apples through the bags on days 2, 3, 5 and 7. Each time, write a word or two for each apple in the table.
flow.say: Let's look at our apples. Don't open the bags. Which ones have changed? Where on the apple did the change start?
flow.kid: Look at each apple through its bag. Don't open it. Write what you see. Where did the change start?
flow.wait: Do this step again on days 2, 3, 5 and 7.
flow.parent: Keep the bags somewhere warm and out of direct sun, not in the fridge, because microbes grow slowly in the cold. A cut apple goes a little brown quickly even without microbes, because the air reacts with it. Rotting is different: the apple goes soft, wet and dark around the cut, and mould may appear. That is what microbes do. If nothing has gone soft by day 7, keep looking for a few more days.
flow.context: This is step 4 of 6 of The Apple Skin Test. In this experiment you test four apples. One has its skin whole, and three have a small cut. You watch them for about a week to see which go bad first. It shows how skin keeps germs out.

flow.do: On day 7, compare all four apples together.
flow.say: Look at all four apples. Which stayed freshest? Which went bad first? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Look at all four. Which one stayed fresh? Which one went bad first? Was your guess right?

check.q: In the apple skin test, apple A (skin whole) stayed fresh longest. What does that tell us?
options: Unbroken skin keeps microbes out
Apples never rot
Apple A was the strongest apple
check.why: All four apples were the same, except for their skin. The one with whole skin stayed fresh, so the skin must keep out the microbes that cause rotting. Your skin does the same job. Picking 'strongest apple' is a guess about the apple, but the fair test tells us it was the skin that made the difference.

flow.context: This is step 5 of 6 of The Apple Skin Test. In this experiment you test four apples. One has its skin whole, and three have a small cut. You watch them for about a week to see which go bad first. It shows how skin keeps germs out.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: skin keeps germs out, and washing a cut helps. What I saw: apple A stayed fresh, apple C went soft first, starting at the cut, and apple D went soft later than C. Why: the cut let microbes in, and washing took many of them away. Throw the closed bags away without opening them.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Apple Skin Test. In this experiment you test four apples. One has its skin whole, and three have a small cut. You watch them for about a week to see which go bad first. It shows how skin keeps germs out.

experiments.title: My Temperature Through the Day
experiments.context: In this experiment you take your own temperature at different times of one day, with a digital thermometer. You find out what 'normal' is for you, so you will know a fever when you see one.
experiments.question: Is my body temperature the same all day? What is normal for me?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will your temperature be the same all day? Will it be higher after running about? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, measure the same way every time: the same thermometer, under the same arm, held for the same time until it beeps. Do not measure straight after a hot bath or a cold drink.
results_table: What I had just been doing

materials.item: a digital thermometer (not a glass mercury one)
a clock or a phone to see the time
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Use only a digital thermometer. Old glass thermometers can break and they hold mercury, which is poisonous. Wipe the tip clean before and after each use.

schedule.what: Measure your temperature in the morning, after playing, in the afternoon and in the evening. Write each one down. Draw a line chart.

experiments.record: Write each temperature in the table. Then make a line chart: time along the bottom, temperature up the side.

flow.kid: This is a thermometer. It tells how hot your body is. Today you find out your normal number.

ask.q: Do you think your temperature is the same all day?
good: I think it changes a little.
Maybe it goes up when I run.

flow.context: This is the first step of My Temperature Through the Day. In this experiment you take your own temperature at different times of one day, with a digital thermometer. You find out what 'normal' is for you, so you will know a fever when you see one.
