check.q: The thermometer reads 36.7 degrees Celsius. Is that a fever?
options: No, it is normal
Yes, it is a high fever
Yes, it is a small fever
check.why: Normal body temperature is around 36 to 37 degrees Celsius. Doctors usually call 38 degrees or more a fever. So 36.7 is normal. Picking 'fever' often means thinking any number above 36 is too hot.

flow.parent: Under the arm reads a little lower than in the mouth. That's fine, as long as you measure the same way each time.

flow.say: Let's measure again after you have run about or jumped for a few minutes. Then this afternoon, and after dinner. Remember to sit still for a few minutes first, and measure the same way.
flow.kid: Measure again: after playing, in the afternoon and in the evening. Same arm, same way. Write each number.
flow.wait: Come back to this step later in the day.

experiments.title: The Sticky Nose Test
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a model of the sticky mucus inside your nose. You put a card with sticky tape and a card with smooth tape near a window, and count how much dust each one traps.
experiments.question: Does a sticky surface, like the mucus in your nose, trap more dust than a dry one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which card will catch more dust specks: the sticky one or the smooth one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two cards the same size, with the same tape, in the same place, for the same time. Only one thing changes: on one card the sticky side of the tape faces up.

materials.item: two white index cards or pieces of stiff white paper
clear sticky tape
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in
a pencil and a ruler

experiments.safety: Wash hands after handling the dusty cards. Put the cards where a baby or a pet cannot reach them.

schedule.what: Make the two cards: sticky tape facing up on one, smooth tape facing up on the other. Lay both flat near an open window.
Turn each card over and tap it once. Count the dust specks between the lines on each card with a magnifying glass. Make a bar chart.

experiments.record: Count the dust specks between the lines on each card twice, and write the counts in the table. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each card.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: dust specks caught in one day
example_chart.y: Number of specks between the lines
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Two white cards, each with a strip of clear tape across it and two pencil lines 4 cm apart. On one card the tape's sticky side faces up, held down at its ends by two small bits of tape.
setup.caption: 1. Put tape sticky side up on one card. Put tape smooth side up on the other.

setup.art: The two cards lying flat side by side on a windowsill next to an open window, taped down at their corners.
setup.caption: 2. Lay both cards flat by an open window. Leave them for a day.

setup.art: A child looking through a magnifying glass at specks of dust stuck on the sticky tape between two pencil lines.
setup.caption: 3. Count the specks between the lines with a magnifying glass.

flow.do: Ask your child to breathe in through their nose and think about where the dust in the air goes.
flow.say: The air we breathe has dust in it, and germs ride on the dust. Inside your nose are tiny hairs and sticky mucus. Today we'll make a pretend nose and test if sticky catches more.
flow.kid: The air has dust in it. Germs ride on dust. Your nose has hairs and sticky mucus. Guess: does sticky catch more dust?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Sticky Nose Test. In this experiment you make a model of the sticky mucus inside your nose. You put a card with sticky tape and a card with smooth tape near a window, and count how much dust each one traps.

flow.do: 1. Stick a strip of clear tape about 8 cm long across each card. On card 1, lay it sticky side up and hold its two ends down with small bits of tape. On card 2, stick it down the normal way, smooth side up. 2. Draw two pencil lines 4 cm apart across each strip. 3. Lay both cards flat by an open window, and tape their corners down.
flow.say: This sticky tape is like the mucus in your nose. The smooth tape is like a nose with no mucus. Both go in the same place for the same time, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: Stick tape sticky side up on one card. Stick tape smooth side up on the other. Draw two lines on each. Put both by an open window.
flow.wait: Leave the cards for one day.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 5 of The Sticky Nose Test. In this experiment you make a model of the sticky mucus inside your nose. You put a card with sticky tape and a card with smooth tape near a window, and count how much dust each one traps.
flow.parent: Count only between the two lines, so both cards are counted over the same area. If the sticky card has fewer than 10 specks after a day, leave both cards one more day.

flow.do: Hold each card upside down and tap it once, so loose dust falls off. Then count the specks between the lines on each card with the magnifying glass, twice. Write both counts, then the number halfway between them.
flow.say: First we turn each card over and tap it. Air rushes through your nose with every breath. Only dust that stays stuck has really been trapped. Now let's count the specks between the lines on each card. Count twice, because it's easy to miss some. Then we find the number halfway between the two counts.
flow.kid: Turn each card over and tap it once. Use the magnifying glass. Count the specks between the lines. Count twice. Write the numbers.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.context: This is step 3 of 5 of The Sticky Nose Test. In this experiment you make a model of the sticky mucus inside your nose. You put a card with sticky tape and a card with smooth tape near a window, and count how much dust each one traps.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart, one bar for each card.
flow.say: Draw a bar for each card. Make it as tall as the number of specks.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each card. The taller bar caught more dust.

check.q: In the sticky nose test, the sticky card caught many more specks than the smooth card. What does that show about mucus?
options: Sticky mucus traps dust and germs before they go deeper
Mucus makes dust
Dry noses are healthier
check.why: Both cards were in the same place for the same time. Only the stickiness was different. So stickiness must trap more dust. Mucus does the same in your nose, catching dust and germs before they reach your lungs. Picking 'mucus makes dust' mixes up catching something with making it.

chart.title: Made-up example: dust specks caught in one day
chart.y: Number of specks between the lines

flow.context: This is step 4 of 5 of The Sticky Nose Test. In this experiment you make a model of the sticky mucus inside your nose. You put a card with sticky tape and a card with smooth tape near a window, and count how much dust each one traps.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: I think sticky mucus traps dust. I saw 42 specks on the sticky card and only 6 on the smooth card. Because dust that touches something sticky stays there. Then ask: so what should we do with what we blow out of our nose? (Blow into a hanky or tissue, throw the tissue away, wash hands.)
flow.context: This is the last step of The Sticky Nose Test. In this experiment you make a model of the sticky mucus inside your nose. You put a card with sticky tape and a card with smooth tape near a window, and count how much dust each one traps.

activities.title: Onion Tears
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity. A grown-up cuts an onion, and you notice what your eyes do. It shows that tears are a defence, not just for crying.

materials.item: one onion
a knife and a chopping board, used only by a grown-up
a hand mirror

activities.safety: Only a grown-up uses the knife. Do not rub your eyes with onion on your hands. If they sting, step away and blink.

schedule.what: Watch a grown-up cut an onion. Notice what your eyes do. Talk about why.

activities.record: Draw your eye before and after the onion. Write one sentence about what your tears did.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting an onion on a wooden board while a child stands at arm's length watching.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts an onion. Stand close enough to smell it.

setup.art: A child looking into a hand mirror, eyes shiny and watery, blinking.
setup.caption: 2. Look in a mirror. What are your eyes doing?

setup.art: A zoomed-in eye with a thin layer of tears sweeping a tiny cloud of onion gas towards the corner.
setup.caption: 3. Tears wash away the stinging gas.

flow.do: Cut an onion in half and then into slices, with your child standing nearby.
flow.say: I'm going to cut an onion. Stand here and watch. Don't touch your eyes. Just notice what happens to them.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts an onion. Stand near and watch. Don't touch your eyes. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: Why do onions make us cry?

flow.context: This is the first step of Onion Tears. This is a short noticing activity. A grown-up cuts an onion, and you notice what your eyes do. It shows that tears are a defence, not just for crying.

flow.do: Hand your child the mirror. Then explain what the tears are doing.
flow.say: Cut onions let out an invisible gas that stings the eyes. Your eyes don't wait for you to decide. They make extra tears straight away and wash the gas out. Tears are a wall that is always on guard. They wash dust and germs away too, every time you blink. They even hold a chemical that breaks some germs open.
flow.kid: Look in the mirror. Your eyes made tears by themselves. Tears wash out the stinging gas. They wash out dust and germs too.

check.q: A grown-up cut an onion near you, and your eyes filled with tears. Why?
options: To wash out the stinging gas
Because you were sad
Because onions are made of water
check.why: Tears are a defence. When something stings or lands in the eye, the eye makes extra tears to wash it out. You weren't sad. Picking 'sad' shows we often think tears are only for feelings. In fact your eyes make tears all day, and every blink spreads them.

flow.think: Your eyes washed themselves without asking you. What else does your body do to protect you without asking?
flow.context: This is the last step of Onion Tears. This is a short noticing activity. A grown-up cuts an onion, and you notice what your eyes do. It shows that tears are a defence, not just for crying.

activities.title: Look at Your Skin Wall
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at your own skin with a magnifying glass. You use sticky tape to pick up old skin flakes, which shows how skin keeps renewing its outer wall.

materials.item: a magnifying glass
clear sticky tape
a piece of black paper

activities.safety: Press the tape gently. Do this on skin with no cuts or rashes.

schedule.what: Look at your skin. Lift skin flakes with tape. Stick them on black paper and look again.

activities.record: Stick your tape on black paper. Label it 'my old wall'. Draw what you saw through the magnifying glass.

setup.art: A child holding a magnifying glass over the back of their hand, showing fine lines and tiny hairs.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the back of your hand with a magnifying glass.

setup.art: A strip of clear tape pressed on a child's forearm, then peeled off.
setup.caption: 2. Press clear tape on your arm. Peel it off.

setup.art: The tape stuck on black paper, with tiny white flakes showing up on it.
setup.caption: 3. Stick the tape on black paper. See the tiny white flakes?

flow.do: Give your child the magnifying glass and ask them to look at their hand, wrist and fingertip.
flow.say: Look closely at your skin. It is not smooth. You can see lines and tiny hairs. On your fingertips you may see tiny dots where sweat comes out. All of this is your outer wall against germs.
flow.kid: Look at your skin with the magnifying glass. Find lines, tiny hairs and tiny dots.

good: It has lines like a net.

flow.context: This is the first step of Look at Your Skin Wall. In this activity you look closely at your own skin with a magnifying glass. You use sticky tape to pick up old skin flakes, which shows how skin keeps renewing its outer wall.

flow.do: 1. Press a strip of tape on the forearm. 2. Peel it off. 3. Stick it on black paper. 4. Look with the magnifying glass.
flow.say: Let's peel off some of the wall. Those tiny white flakes are dead skin cells. Your skin's top layer is made of flat dead cells packed tight, like tiles on a roof. New cells grow underneath and push up. The old ones flake off and take germs with them.
flow.kid: Press tape on your arm. Peel it off. Stick it on black paper. The white flakes are old skin cells.

check.q: You pressed tape on your arm and stuck it on black paper. What are the tiny white flakes on it?
options: Dead skin cells from the top layer
Germs
Dust from the air
check.why: The top layer of skin is made of flat, dead cells. They are always being pushed up from below and flaking off. Germs are far too small to see with a magnifying glass. Picking 'germs' is a common guess, but you would need a microscope to see them.

flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Look at Your Skin Wall. In this activity you look closely at your own skin with a magnifying glass. You use sticky tape to pick up old skin flakes, which shows how skin keeps renewing its outer wall.
flow.parent: If you see only a few flakes, try the back of the hand or the elbow, where skin is drier.

flow.do: Talk about what makes the wall strong and what breaks it.
flow.say: Your skin wall keeps germs out as long as it has no holes. What could make a hole in it?
flow.kid: Your skin keeps germs out. What could make a hole in it? Say three things.

ask.q: What could break the skin wall?
What should we do if it breaks?
good: Cover it with a clean plaster.

flow.context: This is the last step of Look at Your Skin Wall. In this activity you look closely at your own skin with a magnifying glass. You use sticky tape to pick up old skin flakes, which shows how skin keeps renewing its outer wall.

activities.title: Be a Phagocyte
activities.context: In this activity you act out how a white blood cell eats a germ. Your hand, inside a sock, is the white blood cell. Balls of scrunched paper are the germs. Bottle caps are the body's own cells.

materials.item: an old sock
10 balls of scrunched newspaper (the germs)
10 bottle caps, or 10 big dried beans like rajma (the body's own cells)
a tray or a big plate (the blood), and a small bowl for the eaten germs

activities.safety: No safety worries. Keep small balls away from babies.

schedule.what: Use a sock-hand white blood cell to find the paper-ball germs by touch, and leave the body's own cells alone.

activities.record: Draw the three steps of a white blood cell eating a germ: touch, wrap, swallow.

setup.art: A child's hand inside an old sock, the sock shaped like a soft blob with wiggly fingers.
setup.caption: 1. Put a sock on your hand. You are a white blood cell.

setup.art: A tray with crumpled newspaper balls (germs) and smooth bottle caps (body cells) mixed together.
setup.caption: 2. Mix the germs and the body's own cells in a tray.

setup.art: The sock hand closed tightly round a crumpled paper ball, then dropping it into a small bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Find a germ by feel. Wrap round it. Drop it in the bowl: it has been eaten.

flow.do: 1. Mix the paper balls and the bottle caps in the tray. 2. Give your child the sock to wear like a glove. 3. Put the small bowl next to the tray.
flow.say: The tray is your blood. The bottle caps are your own body's cells. The paper balls are germs that got in through a cut. Your sock hand is a white blood cell called a phagocyte. That means 'eating cell'.
flow.kid: The tray is your blood. Bottle caps are your own cells. Paper balls are germs. Your sock hand is a white blood cell. White blood cells eat germs!
flow.context: This is the first step of Be a Phagocyte. In this activity you act out how a white blood cell eats a germ. Your hand, inside a sock, is the white blood cell. Small balls of paper are the germs.

flow.do: Ask your child to close their eyes, feel for germs, and wrap the sock hand round each one. Each wrapped germ goes in the bowl.
flow.say: A white blood cell has no eyes. They find germs by touch and by chemical smells. Close your eyes. Feel each thing in the tray. Germs feel crumpled. Your own cells feel smooth. When you find a germ, close your sock hand round them and drop it in the bowl. Leave the smooth ones alone.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Feel the things in the tray. Germs feel crumpled. Your own cells feel smooth. Wrap your sock round a germ. Drop it in the bowl.
flow.parent: Feeling crumpled or smooth stands for the shapes on a germ's surface. Real white blood cells recognise germs by touch, when shapes fit together like a key in a lock.

check.q: How does a real white blood cell find a germ?
options: They follow chemical signals and feel the germ's shapes
They see the germ with tiny eyes
They hear the germ moving
check.why: A white blood cell has no eyes or ears. Hurt cells give off chemical signals, and the white blood cell crawls towards them. When they touch a germ, shapes on the germ fit shapes on the cell, like a key in a lock. Picking 'eyes' is a natural guess, because that is how we find things.

flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Be a Phagocyte. In this activity you act out how a white blood cell eats a germ. Your hand, inside a sock, is the white blood cell. Small balls of paper are the germs.

flow.do: Count the germs swallowed. Then talk about what happens next.
flow.say: How many germs are in the bowl? Inside a real white blood cell, the germ is broken down by strong chemicals. After a lot of eating, the white blood cell often dies. A heap of dead white blood cells and germs is pus.
flow.kid: Count the germs in the bowl. Inside a real cell, the germ is broken down. Tired cells die. A heap of them is pus.

ask.q: Did you wrap any bottle caps by mistake?
good: Yes, one. Real cells try very hard not to do that.

flow.think: Sometimes real white blood cells attack the body's own cells by mistake. Scientists call this an autoimmune illness. Why might it be hard to tell germs from your own cells?
flow.context: This is the last step of Be a Phagocyte. In this activity you act out how a white blood cell eats a germ. Your hand, inside a sock, is the white blood cell. Small balls of paper are the germs.

activities.title: Count Your Blinks
activities.context: In this activity you count how many times a person blinks in one minute. Every blink spreads a fresh layer of tears that washes the eye.

materials.item: a clock, a sand timer or a phone timer
a pencil and paper for tally marks

schedule.what: Count blinks in one minute while talking, then while reading or watching a screen.

activities.record: Make tally marks for each blink. Write the totals for talking and for reading.

setup.art: Two children facing each other, one talking, the other making tally marks on paper with a timer beside them.
setup.caption: 1. One person talks for a minute. The other counts their blinks.

setup.art: A child reading a book while another child watches their eyes and makes tally marks.
setup.caption: 2. Count again while they read or look at a screen.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer for one minute. 2. Have a chat while your child counts your blinks with tally marks. 3. Swap.
flow.say: Every time you blink, your eyelid spreads a fresh layer of tears across your eye, like a wiper on a windscreen. Let's count how often that happens. I'll talk for one minute. You make a tally mark every time I blink.
flow.kid: Watch a grown-up's eyes for one minute. Make a tally mark every time they blink.

chart.title: Made-up example: blinks in one minute

flow.context: This is the first step of Count Your Blinks. In this activity you count how many times a person blinks in one minute. Every blink spreads a fresh layer of tears that washes the eye.

flow.do: Count again while the person reads silently, then compare.
flow.say: Now let's count while you read. Do you think the number will be the same?
flow.kid: Count blinks again while someone reads. Is the number the same?

check.q: People usually blink less while reading or looking at a screen. What might that do to their eyes?
options: Their eyes may get dry and tired, with fewer tear washes
Their eyes get cleaner
Nothing at all
check.why: Each blink spreads tears that wash and wet the eye. Fewer blinks means fewer washes, so the eyes can feel dry and tired. That is why doctors say to look away from a screen and blink every so often. Picking 'cleaner' misses that the blink is what does the cleaning.

flow.think: People blink about 15 to 20 times a minute when talking. How many times might you blink in a whole day?
flow.context: This is the last step of Count Your Blinks. In this activity you count how many times a person blinks in one minute. Every blink spreads a fresh layer of tears that washes the eye.

activities.title: The Lizard's Fever
activities.context: In this activity you act out a real experiment. Scientists found that sick lizards move to warm places and give themselves a fever. It shows that fever is a very old defence.

materials.item: a warm spot and a cool spot, such as a patch of sun by a window and a shady corner
a towel to be a warm rock

activities.safety: Do not stay in hot sun for long. Drink water after.

schedule.what: Act out healthy and sick lizards choosing warm and cool spots. Talk about fever.

activities.record: Draw a lizard on a warm rock. Write: 'Sick lizards warm up, because…'

setup.art: A room with a sunny patch by a window and a shady corner, and a towel laid in the sun like a warm rock.
setup.caption: 1. Find a warm spot and a cool spot.

setup.art: A child crawling like a lizard towards the towel in the sun, with a thermometer drawn above showing it rising.
setup.caption: 2. As a 'sick lizard', crawl to the warm rock.

flow.do: Ask your child to crawl about as a healthy lizard, moving between sun and shade.
flow.say: Lizards make very little heat of their own. To warm up, they lie on a hot rock. To cool down, they hide in shade. Be a healthy lizard. Move between sun and shade.
flow.kid: You are a lizard. Lizards warm up on hot rocks and cool down in shade. Move between sun and shade.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Lizard's Fever. In this activity you act out a real experiment. Scientists found that sick lizards move to warm places and give themselves a fever. It shows that fever is a very old defence.

flow.do: Say 'Now you are a sick lizard' and see where your child goes. Then tell them about the experiment.
flow.say: Now you are a sick lizard. Germs got in. In the 1970s, a scientist called Matthew Kluger watched sick desert lizards. They crawled to warmer spots than healthy ones. They gave themselves a fever! And sick lizards kept in a cool place were more likely to die. So fever is not a mistake. It is one of the oldest defences on Earth. Fish and insects do it too.
flow.kid: Now you are a sick lizard. Where do you go? Real sick lizards crawl to the warm rock. They give themselves a fever. It helps them fight germs.

check.q: In an experiment, sick lizards moved to warmer spots than healthy lizards did. What does this tell us?
options: Fever is an old defence that helps fight germs
Lizards like the sun when they are bored
Fever only happens in people
check.why: Lizards make very little heat of their own, so they choose warm spots to raise their temperature when they are sick. Those that could warm up survived better. This shows fever is a defence that animals have had for a very long time. Picking 'only in people' is natural, because we notice our own fevers most.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Lizard's Fever. In this activity you act out a real experiment. Scientists found that sick lizards move to warm places and give themselves a fever. It shows that fever is a very old defence.

activities.title: Draw the Hidden Fight
activities.context: In this activity you draw a model: what you think is happening under the skin of a scraped knee, including the parts you can't see. Scientists draw models like this to explain ideas.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper
coloured pencils or crayons

schedule.what: Draw a big scraped knee from the side, with skin, germs, blood vessels and white blood cells. Label everything.

activities.record: Label your drawing: skin, cut, germs, blood vessel, white blood cell, pus, scab.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper showing a side view of skin like stacked tiles with a gap (the cut) and a red tube underneath.
setup.caption: 1. Draw skin from the side, with a cut in it and a blood vessel below.

setup.art: The same drawing with small green germs entering the gap and round white blood cells squeezing out of the red tube towards them.
setup.caption: 2. Add germs coming in, and white blood cells coming out of the blood.

setup.art: The finished drawing with a scab like a lid on top, and labels with arrows.
setup.caption: 3. Add a scab on top. Label every part.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a scraped knee from the side, as if it were cut in half. Show the skin and a blood vessel.
flow.say: Let's draw what we can't see. Imagine we sliced the knee and looked from the side. Draw the skin like a row of tiles, with a gap where it's scraped. Underneath, draw a blood vessel, a tube that carries blood. Now draw germs coming in. Where do the white blood cells come from?
flow.kid: Draw a scraped knee from the side. Draw the skin like tiles, with a gap. Draw a blood vessel under it. Add germs coming in. Where do the white blood cells come from?

ask.q: Why does the skin around the cut go red and warm?
good: More blood comes to bring white blood cells.

flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Hidden Fight. In this activity you draw a model: what you think is happening under the skin of a scraped knee, including the parts you can't see. Scientists draw models like this to explain ideas.

flow.do: Ask your child to add white blood cells, pus and a scab, and label everything.
flow.say: Draw white blood cells squeezing out of the blood vessel and eating germs. Draw some tired ones in a pile. That's pus. Now draw a scab on top, like a lid. New skin will grow underneath.
flow.kid: Draw white blood cells eating germs. Draw a pile of tired ones: that's pus. Draw a scab on top like a lid. Label it all.

check.q: What is a scab on a scraped knee for?
options: It seals the hole while new skin grows underneath
It is where the germs live
It is dead germs
check.why: A scab is dried blood and a sticky mesh. It closes the hole in the skin wall, so fewer germs get in while new skin grows below. That is why we don't pick scabs. Picking 'where germs live' is a common worry, but a clean scab is a lid, not a germ nest.

flow.parent: There is no single right drawing. Look for a wall with a gap, germs getting in, white blood cells coming from the blood, and a scab sealing it. Praise any label the child explains in their own words.
flow.context: This is the last step of Draw the Hidden Fight. In this activity you draw a model: what you think is happening under the skin of a scraped knee, including the parts you can't see. Scientists draw models like this to explain ideas.

projects.title: Build the Body Castle
projects.context: In this 2-day project you build a cardboard castle that shows all the body's defences: walls, gates, guards and a heat knob. Then you give a tour of it to your family.

materials.item: a big cardboard box
scissors, glue, tape and coloured paper
cotton wool, a little honey or glue for 'mucus', and blue cellophane or plastic for 'tears'
small balls of paper as germs and cotton balls as white blood cells
a paper dial for the fever knob, with a split pin

projects.safety: A grown-up helps with sharp scissors and cutting cardboard.

schedule.what: Plan the castle on paper. Build the outer wall (skin) and the gates (eyes, nose, mouth) with their defences.
Add the inside guards (white blood cells), a cut in the wall, and the fever knob. Give a family tour.

projects.record: Take a photo or draw your castle. Write one sentence for each defence on a label.

setup.art: A child drawing a castle plan on paper with labels: skin wall, eye gate, nose gate, mouth gate, guards, heat knob.
setup.caption: 1. Plan your castle on paper first.

setup.art: A cardboard box castle with a paper skin wall, an eye window with blue cellophane tears, a nose gate with cotton hairs and a mouth gate.
setup.caption: 2. Build the wall and the gates with their defences.

setup.art: Inside the castle: cotton-ball guards on a red paper road, paper-ball germs near a cut in the wall, and a paper dial knob on the tower.
setup.caption: 3. Add the guards inside, a cut in the wall, and a fever knob.

flow.do: Help your child plan the castle on paper: which part is which defence.
flow.say: Your body is defended like a castle. Let's plan one. What is the outer wall? What are the gates? Who guards the gates? Who are the soldiers inside?
flow.kid: Plan a castle that is a body. The wall is skin. The gates are eyes, nose and mouth. Who guards each gate? Draw a plan.
flow.context: This is the first step of Build the Body Castle. In this 2-day project you build a cardboard castle that shows all the body's defences: walls, gates, guards and a heat knob. Then you give a tour of it to your family.

flow.do: Build the wall and gates from the box. Add tears at the eye window, and hairs and 'mucus' at the nose gate. Put a label for stomach acid behind the mouth gate.
flow.say: Let's build the walls. Use blue plastic for tears at the eye windows. Cotton for nose hairs. A little honey for sticky mucus. Label each one.
flow.kid: Build the castle wall and gates. Blue plastic for tears. Cotton for nose hairs. A dab of honey for mucus. Label each one.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the cardboard. The child decides where things go and writes the labels.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 4 of Build the Body Castle. In this 2-day project you build a cardboard castle that shows all the body's defences: walls, gates, guards and a heat knob. Then you give a tour of it to your family.

flow.do: On day 2, cut a small 'wound' in the wall and put germs at it. Make cotton-ball guards on a red paper road.
flow.say: Oh no, a cut in the wall! Germs are getting in. Where do the guards come from? Let's lay a red road for the blood, and put the white blood cell guards on it.
flow.kid: Make a cut in the wall. Put germs there. Make a red road for blood. Put cotton-ball guards on it, rushing to the cut.

check.q: Body castle: germs got through a cut in the wall. Who comes to fight them?
options: White blood cells, through the blood
Tears from the eyes
Saliva from the mouth
check.why: Once germs are through the skin, the inside defenders take over. White blood cells travel in the blood and squeeze out where they are needed. Tears and saliva guard only the eyes and mouth. Picking them is thinking all defences are the same, but each one guards its own place.

flow.context: This is step 3 of 4 of Build the Body Castle. In this 2-day project you build a cardboard castle that shows all the body's defences: walls, gates, guards and a heat knob. Then you give a tour of it to your family.

flow.do: Fix a paper fever knob on the tower and invite the family for a tour.
flow.say: The brain's heat knob sits on the tower. When the guards call for help, the knob turns up. That's a fever. Now give your family a tour of the castle.
flow.kid: Put a heat knob on the tower. Turn it up when the guards call: that's a fever. Now give your family a tour!
flow.parent: During the tour, ask a visiting family member to ask 'How do you know?' about one defence.
flow.context: This is the last step of Build the Body Castle. In this 2-day project you build a cardboard castle that shows all the body's defences: walls, gates, guards and a heat knob. Then you give a tour of it to your family.

challenges.title: The Sneeze Stopper
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A spray bottle makes a pretend sneeze. You test ways to catch it, and design the best sneeze stopper you can.
challenges.problem: A sneeze can spray tiny drops, carrying germs, a long way. Use a spray bottle as a pretend sneeze. Find the best way to stop the drops reaching a paper 'friend' 1 metre away.
constraints: The sneezer must still be able to breathe and see.
Test each idea the same way: 3 sprays from the same place, 1 metre from the paper.
materials: a spray bottle with water and a few drops of food colouring or ink
a big sheet of white paper taped to a wall
a tissue, a hanky, a cloth mask, paper and your own elbow (sleeve)
general: Sneeze into a tissue, then throw the tissue away and wash your hands.

quiz.p: Ravi, a boy in Class 3, says the immune system is one organ, like the heart. Is he right?
opts: Yes. It sits in the chest
No. It is many parts working together, like skin, tears, mucus, white blood cells and fever
Yes. It is the stomach
quiz.why: The immune system is not one organ. It is everything the body does to keep germs out and to fight the ones that get in.

quiz.p: Germs on an unwashed guava go into your mouth. Saliva washes some of them down. Which wall do the swallowed germs meet next?
opts: Tears
Nose hairs
Stomach acid
quiz.why: The acid in the stomach kills many germs that come in with food. Tears guard the eyes, and nose hairs guard the nose.

quiz.p: Why do your eyes fill with tears when someone cuts an onion near you?
opts: You feel sad
Tears wash out the stinging gas
Onions are full of water that jumps into your eyes
Your eyes are tired
quiz.why: Tears are a defence that washes the eye. Cut onions give off a gas that stings, so the eyes make extra tears. Picking 'sad' shows we often think tears are only for feelings.
quiz.context: This question is about the onion tears activity.

quiz.p: When you have a cold, your nose runs with extra mucus. How might that help you?
opts: The extra mucus traps germs and carries them out
The extra mucus feeds the germs
It does not help at all
quiz.why: Mucus is a sticky trap. More mucus means more germs are caught and blown out or swallowed. A runny nose is annoying, but it is part of the fight.

quiz.p: White blood cells and red blood cells both travel in the blood. Which job belongs to white blood cells?
opts: Carrying oxygen round the body
Finding germs and destroying them
Making the skin white
quiz.why: White blood cells hunt germs. Red blood cells carry oxygen. Picking 'making the skin white' comes from the name, but white blood cells have nothing to do with skin colour.

quiz.p: A splinter goes into a girl's finger. Which sign shows that her body is fighting germs at that spot?
opts: Her finger turns blue and cold
Nothing changes at all
Her finger goes red, warm and a little puffy
quiz.why: Redness, warmth and swelling are inflammation: more blood brings white blood cells to the spot. This is what Élie Metchnikoff saw round the thorn in the starfish.

quiz.p: What does a phagocyte do when they touch a germ?
opts: Wraps round the germ and swallows them
Runs away from the germ
Turns into a germ
quiz.why: A phagocyte is a white blood cell that eats germs. They wrap round the germ, pull them inside and break them down with chemicals.

quiz.p: A child's temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius in the morning and 37.2 after playing. Does the child have a fever?
opts: Yes, because it went up
No. Both are normal, and a fever is 38 or more
Yes, because anything above 37 is a fever
quiz.why: A small change through the day is normal, and playing makes heat. Doctors usually call 38 degrees Celsius or more a fever.

quiz.p: A child has a fever. Which of these means a grown-up should call a doctor quickly?
opts: The child feels warm and sleepy for one evening
The child wants water
The child has a stiff neck and a new rash
The child wants a blanket
quiz.why: A doctor is needed for a stiff neck, a rash, trouble breathing or a fit. A doctor is also needed for a fever of 40 degrees or more, one lasting more than 3 days, or any fever in a baby under 3 months. Feeling warm, sleepy and thirsty is common in an ordinary fever.

quiz.p: In the apple skin test, why did we keep everything the same except the skin?
opts: To make it quicker
So we could be sure the skin made the difference
Because apples are all the same anyway
So the apples taste the same
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Then, if the results differ, we know what caused it. Picking 'apples are all the same' misses why we chose them carefully.
quiz.context: This question is about the apple skin test, with four apples sealed in bags.

quiz.p: Curd is full of microbes. Is eating curd harmful?
opts: Yes. All microbes are germs
No. The microbes in curd are friendly, and many friendly microbes live in our gut and help us
Only if the curd is cold
quiz.why: Only a few microbes are germs. The ones that turn milk into curd are friendly. Picking 'all microbes are germs' is the most common idea, and many adverts encourage it.

quiz.p: A chemical in tears, called lysozyme, protects you by…
opts: Making your eyes see better
Turning tears salty
Breaking open the outer coat of some bacteria
Feeding friendly microbes
quiz.why: Lysozyme fits a part of a bacterium's coat, like a key in a lock, and snips it so the bacterium bursts. Alexander Fleming found it in 1921.

quiz.p: When a neem tree is cut, sticky gum oozes out and hardens over the cut. Which of your body's defences is this most like?
opts: A sneeze
A scab sealing a cut
Crying
quiz.why: Both the gum and the scab seal a hole in the outer wall, so germs cannot get in while it heals. Trees have no blood, but they defend themselves too.

applications: Doctors wash their hands and wear gloves, so they do not carry germs through a patient's broken skin.
First aid: washing a scrape with clean water and covering it with a clean plaster helps the skin wall heal.
Thermometers at home and in clinics tell families when a child has a fever.
Hospitals count white blood cells in a blood test. Too many or too few can tell a doctor that the body is fighting something.
Vaccines teach white blood cells to recognise a germ safely. You will learn how in Class 4.
Masks and covering sneezes stop germs travelling in drops from one person to the next.
Food safety: cooking, boiling water and keeping food covered help stomach acid by sending fewer germs down.
Eye drops that are like tears help people whose eyes do not make enough tears.
Lysozyme from egg white is used to help keep some foods, like some cheeses, from spoiling.
Plant scientists breed crops with stronger natural defences, so farmers need fewer sprays.
Scientists use the CRISPR system, borrowed from the defences of bacteria, as a tool to edit genes.
Doctors grow and study white blood cells in labs to find new treatments for illnesses.

open_questions.q: Why does the same germ make one person very ill and another hardly ill at all?
open_questions.why_open: Genes, age, sleep, food, earlier illnesses and luck all seem to play a part. Scientists are still working out how they fit together.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does the immune system decide what is 'me' and what is 'not me'?
open_questions.why_open: There are strong ideas, like learning 'self' early and listening for danger signals. But nobody has the full answer yet.

open_questions.q: How does the immune system talk to the brain, and make us feel tired and grumpy when ill?
open_questions.why_open: Chemicals from white blood cells reach the brain. Scientists think this makes us rest, but how it all works is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Is bringing a fever down good, bad or neither for getting better?
open_questions.why_open: Studies give mixed answers. Fever helps animals survive infections, but fever medicines in children do not seem to make illnesses much longer.

open_questions.q: Why do some immune systems attack harmless things, like pollen or peanuts?
open_questions.why_open: Allergies have become more common in many countries. Scientists have several ideas, including less contact with harmless microbes when young, but it is not settled.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of white blood cells are there, really?
open_questions.why_open: Every few years scientists find new kinds, or new jobs for old kinds. The list keeps growing.

open_questions.q: Do our friendly microbes change how our immune system works, and even how we feel?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments in mice suggest gut microbes affect the immune system a lot. How much this is true in people is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How did the first living things begin to tell themselves apart from the outside world?
open_questions.why_open: Even the oldest cells had a skin, a membrane, keeping inside separate from outside. How the first defences began, billions of years ago, is a mystery.

maths.problem: In one family's sticky nose test, the sticky card caught 42 dust specks. The smooth card caught 6. How many more specks did the sticky card catch?
maths.explain: The sticky card caught 42 specks. The smooth card caught 6. 42 take away 6 is 36. So the sticky card caught 36 more. You can check: 6 + 36 = 42.
maths.context: This is about the sticky nose test. You left a sticky tape card and a smooth tape card near a window for a day and counted the dust specks on each.

chart.title: Dust specks caught in one day

maths.why_maths: Saying 'sticky caught more' is a start. Working out how many more tells us how big the difference really is.

maths.problem: In the same test, the sticky card caught 42 specks and the smooth card caught 6. How many times as many specks did the sticky card catch?
maths.explain: 42 divided by 6 is 7. So the sticky card caught 7 times as many specks. Check: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 42.
maths.context: This is about the sticky nose test. A sticky card, like the mucus in your nose, and a smooth tape card were left by a window for a day.
maths.why_maths: Scientists like to say 'how many times better'. Dividing shows how much better sticky mucus is at trapping dust.

maths.problem: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3, measured her temperature. It was 36.3 degrees Celsius at 7 am and 36.9 after running. Later, when she had a cold, it read 38.4. Which of these numbers is a fever?
maths.explain: Doctors usually call 38 degrees Celsius or more a fever. 36.3 and 36.9 are both below 38, so they are normal. 38.4 is more than 38. So 38.4 is a fever. The number after the dot is tenths of a degree: 38.4 is 38 degrees and 4 tenths.
maths.context: This is about the experiment where you took your temperature at different times of day with a digital thermometer.
maths.why_maths: A thermometer only helps if you can read its number and compare it with the fever line at 38.

maths.problem: A mother blinked 18 times in one minute while talking. If she kept blinking at the same speed, how many times would she blink in 5 minutes of talking?
maths.explain: 18 blinks each minute, for 5 minutes. 18 times 5 is 90. You can also add: 18 + 18 + 18 + 18 + 18 = 90. That is 90 fresh washes of tears on each eye.
maths.context: This is about the Count Your Blinks activity, where you counted how many times a person blinked in one minute.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying turns one short count into a picture of a whole day, and shows how often tears wash your eyes.

maths.problem: In one family's apple skin test, apple C first had a soft patch on day 3. Apple D, which was washed, first had a soft patch on day 5. How many days longer did washing keep apple D firm?
maths.explain: Apple C went soft on day 3. Apple D went soft on day 5. 5 take away 3 is 2. So washing kept apple D firm for 2 more days. Washing took away many of the soil microbes, so fewer were left to start the rot. It did not take them all away, because apple D still went soft in the end.
maths.context: This is about the apple skin test. You closed four apples in bags, three with small cuts, and wrote what you saw each time you looked.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'washing helped' is a start. Counting the days shows how much it helped.

maths.problem: In one family's sneeze stopper test, 60 spots landed on the paper with nothing in the way. With a hand in front, 12 landed. With an elbow, 4. Draw a bar chart. How many fewer spots got through with the elbow than with nothing?
maths.explain: With nothing, 60 spots. With the elbow, 4 spots. 60 take away 4 is 56. So 56 fewer spots got through with the elbow. In the bar chart the elbow's bar is much shorter.
maths.context: This is about the sneeze stopper challenge, where a spray bottle was a pretend sneeze and you tested ways to catch the drops.

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which stopper works best, so we can choose the safest way to sneeze.

roots.context: We have been learning how the body keeps germs out and fights the ones that get in. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Every apple in the test had microbes on its skin. The ones that rotted all had cuts, and the rot began at the cut. Unbroken skin kept the microbes out just by being whole. Most of your body's protection works this way, with walls that stop germs before any fight begins.
deep_truth.habit: We picture the immune system as soldiers fighting germs. Most of the work is done before any fight, by skin, tears and mucus that are always there.
deep_truth.evidence: In the apple skin test, the apple with whole skin stayed fresh, while cut apples went soft, starting at the cut. In the sticky nose test, sticky tape held far more dust than smooth tape.

three.who_am_i: Your skin, your tears and the mucus in your nose keep you well every minute, and you hardly notice them.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing, from a bacterium to a neem tree to you, has an outer layer that keeps their inside apart from the outside.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of microbes, on every apple, door handle and breath of air. Most of them never get in, and most would do you no harm.

roots.thread: The first living things were single cells, each wrapped in a thin skin called a membrane. That skin let food in and kept harm out. Your own body began as one cell, and grew into trillions, each still wrapped in their own membrane. Your skin, your tears and your mucus do the same job for the whole body. Life began with one kind of wall, and it has grown into countless kinds, in bacteria, trees and you.

teachings.teaching: The best rulers are hardly noticed by their people. When the work is done, the people say, 'It happened by itself.'
teachings.link: Your skin and tears protect you so quietly that you forget them. In the apple test, the whole skin kept the apple fresh, and nobody saw it doing anything.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, 'interbeing', in his book The Heart of Understanding (1988)
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain and the tree in it. Nothing exists all by itself.
teachings.link: Look deeply at your skin and you can see the friendly microbes that live on it and help guard it. Your wall is made partly of other living things.

teachings.source: Jain anekantavada, the story of the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Each blind man touched one part of the elephant and was sure he knew the whole. Each was partly right.
teachings.link: Metchnikoff said cells fight germs. Ehrlich said chemicals do. They argued for twenty-five years, and they were both partly right.

science.text: Skin, tears, mucus and stomach acid stop most germs before white blood cells are needed. Most germs get in only where a wall is broken, such as a cut or a mosquito bite.
How the immune system decides what is 'self' and what to attack, by learning self early or by listening for danger, is still argued about.

other_view.view: The walls are only half the story. Some germs get past them every day, through the gut, the lungs and tiny scratches. The white blood cells inside, and the way they remember germs, matter just as much. People whose inside defenders do not work well need special care from doctors, even with healthy skin.

practice.title: Notice your walls
practice.say: Let's sit still and close our eyes. Blink slowly three times. Feel your tears spread across your eyes. Now breathe in slowly through your nose. The hairs and mucus inside are cleaning that air right now. Now feel the skin on your arms and face. It is keeping germs out this very moment, and you never asked it to. Sit for one more slow breath.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Blink slowly three times. Feel your tears. Breathe in through your nose. Your nose is cleaning the air. Feel the skin on your arms. It keeps germs out right now.

ask: Your skin keeps germs out all day, and you hardly notice it working. What else in your body works without you noticing?
If a wall stopped everything, what would your body miss out on?
The microbes in the apple test were living things looking for food. Were they doing anything wrong?

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1880s, many scientists thought that germs inside the body were killed only by chemicals in the blood. The body's cells, they said, did nothing useful. In 1882, Élie Metchnikoff pushed rose thorns into see-through baby starfish. By the next morning, wandering cells had crowded round every thorn. In 1884 he watched tiny water fleas that had swallowed the spores of a fungus. When the fleas' cells ate the spores, the flea lived. When the spores grew faster than the cells could eat them, the flea died. Other scientists, such as George Nuttall in 1888, showed that blood with no cells in it could still kill some bacteria. For years, each side said the other was wrong. Then, in 1903, Almroth Wright and Stewart Douglas in London showed that chemicals in the blood coat germs and make them easier for the eating cells to swallow. The chemicals and the cells work together. In 1908, Metchnikoff and Paul Ehrlich, who studied the chemicals, shared the Nobel Prize.
how_we_found_out.who: Élie Metchnikoff, George Nuttall, Almroth Wright and Stewart Douglas
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Germs inside the body are killed only by chemicals in the blood, and the body's cells play no useful part. Metchnikoff watched cells eat germs, and Wright and Douglas showed that the chemicals and the cells work together.
